passages.title: Praise for the flawless Book and its warning
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat are the doorway to Sūrah al-Kahf: a declaration of praise to Allah for sending down a Book in which He placed no flaw, followed by a statement of exactly what that Book was sent to do — to warn of a severe punishment from Allah Himself, to give believers the good news of an everlasting reward, and to confront head-on the gravest lie a tongue can utter: that Allah has taken a child. What binds the passage together is the Book itself. Ayah 1 describes what the Qurʼān *is* (flawless, straight); ayat 2–5 describe what it *does* (warns, gives glad tidings, and refutes). Praise, description, and purpose form one unbroken sentence of glorification.

## The story behind this sūrah

Both Ibn Kathir (through Muhammad bin Ishaq, from ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas) and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (through Ibn Jarir al-Tabari, from Ibn ʿAbbas) relate the occasion on which the sūrah came down — and it is a story worth telling properly, because it explains why the sūrah opens the way it does.

The Quraysh of Makkah, unsettled by the Prophet's ﷺ growing influence, sent two of their men — An-Nadr bin Al-Harith and ʿUqbah bin Abi Muʿit — to the Jewish rabbis in Madinah, reasoning that these were "the people of the first Book" who knew the Prophets better than the Arabs did. The rabbis set a test: ask him three questions. Ask about some young men of ancient times whose tale is strange and wondrous; ask about a man who travelled the east and the west of the earth; and ask about the Rūh — the soul or spirit — what is it? If he answers, he is a Prophet, so follow him; if not, he is inventing things.

The emissaries returned triumphant, announcing "a decisive solution," and the questions were put to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He replied, "I will tell you tomorrow about what you have asked me" — but did not say "if Allah wills." And then, for fifteen days, no revelation came. Jibril did not descend. The Makkans began to taunt him — "Muhammad promised to tell us the next day, and now fifteen days have gone by" — and the Prophet ﷺ was grieved both by the delay in revelation and by what was being said about him.

Then Jibril came with this sūrah. It contained the story of the young men (the People of the Cave, Ashāb al-Kahf) and the great traveller (Dhul-Qarnain); the question about the Rūh had been answered in the ayah "And they ask you concerning the Rūh…" (17:85). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, citing al-Suyuti, that this is why Sūrah al-Kahf sits immediately after Sūrah Banī Isrāʼīl in the mushaf. And it explains the delay itself: because "if Allah wills" had not been said, the revelation was delayed as a measure of reminder — one should say *inshāʼ Allāh* when promising anything in the future, a point the sūrah itself will make explicitly in ayat 23–24.

Read against this backdrop, the opening takes on its full force. After fifteen days of silence and mockery, the revelation that breaks the silence begins: *All praise is due to Allah, Who has sent down to His servant the Book.*

## Why the sūrah opens with praise

Ibn Kathir notes that Allah praises His Holy Self at the beginning and end of matters, for He is the One to be praised in all circumstances. Here He praises Himself specifically for revealing His Mighty Book to His Noble Messenger Muhammad ﷺ — which, Ibn Kathir says, is *the greatest blessing that Allah has granted the people of this earth*, for through the Qurʼān He brings them out of darkness into light. The greatest of all gifts deserves the opening of praise.

## "No crookedness… perfectly straight": two words that carry the passage

The heart of ayah 1 and the first word of ayah 2 form a deliberate pair, and the classical commentators dwell on them.

**ʿIwaj (عوج) — "crookedness."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this means crookedness of any kind: inclination towards one side, deviation from the norms of rectitude. The Qurʼān is free of all of it — in the perfection of its words and of its meanings, admitting no distortion anywhere, "either in eloquence or in knowledge and wisdom." Ibn Kathir puts it simply: there is nothing twisted or confusing about it; it clearly guides to a straight path, plain and manifest.

**Qayyim (قيّم) — "straight," and perhaps more.** Here the negative statement (no crookedness) is immediately fortified by a positive one. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *qayyim* carries the sense of *mustaqīm* — straightforward, upright — and what is truly straight cannot have the least tilt towards any side. But it records a second possible sense as well: *qayyim* can also mean caretaker, custodian, protector. On that reading, the Qurʼān is not only perfect in itself, free of all excess and deficiency — it also *keeps others upright*, firm and unflinching, guarding the interests of all the servants of Allah. Maʿārif (citing Mazhari) draws the two senses together beautifully: the Qurʼān stands perfect in itself, and it has the power to make the men and women who follow it perfect too. The Book is straight, and it straightens.

## The warning and the good news (ayat 2–3)

The straight Book was sent with a double mission, and the passage names the warning first: *to give warning of a severe punishment from Him*. Ibn Kathir explains that this is addressed to those who oppose Allah's Prophet ﷺ and disbelieve in His Book — a punishment that may be hastened in this world and is otherwise postponed to the Hereafter. And the phrase *min ladunhu*, "from Him," is not decoration: it means from Allah Himself, "for none can punish as He punishes and none is stronger or more reliable than Him." A threat is only as weighty as the one who makes it; this one comes from the Lord of all strength.

Then the good news. It is given to "the believers who do righteous deeds" — Ibn Kathir pauses on this pairing: those who believe in the Qurʼān *and confirm their faith by righteous actions*. Faith in this passage is not a bare claim; it is belief made visible in works. For them is *ajran hasanan*, which Ibn Kathir renders "a beautiful reward from Allah" — and ayah 3 completes it: *mākithīna fīhi abadan*, abiding therein forever. "Therein," Ibn Kathir explains, means in that reward, which is Paradise; and *abadan* means for always, "never ending or ceasing to be." Two words, and the entire horizon of the believer's hope: not merely a reward, but one that never runs out.

## The gravest word ever spoken (ayat 4–5)

After the general warning to disbelievers, the passage singles out one group for a warning of its own: *those who say, "Allah has begotten a child."* Ibn Kathir cites Ibn Ishaq that the immediate reference is to the pagan Arabs, who said, "We worship the angels, who are the daughters of Allah."

Ayah 5 then dismantles the claim with three strikes. First: *no knowledge have they of such a thing, nor had their fathers* — the claim is pure fabrication, Ibn Kathir says, and appealing to inherited tradition does not help, because their predecessors knew no better than they do. An old lie is still a lie. Second: *kaburat kalimatan* — "Mighty is the word that comes out of their mouths." Ibn Kathir explains that this phrase highlights the seriousness and enormity of the lie they have made up: it has no basis apart from their own saying of it, and no evidence behind it apart from their own fabrication. The wording is pointed — the claim exists nowhere except as sound leaving their mouths. Third, the verdict: *they utter nothing but a lie.*

This is why the Book's straightness matters. A Book with no crookedness confronts the most crooked of words — and the passage's structure makes the contrast unmissable: the flawless speech of Allah set against a human word so distorted that the Qurʼān measures its sheer enormity before refuting it.

## A shield against the Dajjal: the virtues of these very ayat

Both commentaries open with the special merits the Sunnah attaches to this sūrah — and specifically to its opening ayat, the ones before you.

- Imam Ahmad recorded from Abu ad-Dardāʼ that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever memorizes ten ayat from the beginning of Sūrat al-Kahf will be protected from the Dajjal." Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by Muslim, Abu Dawud, an-Nasaʼi and at-Tirmidhi; in at-Tirmidhi's version it is "three ayat from the beginning of al-Kahf," and he graded it "Hasan Sahih." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that a report from the same authority in the same books says the like about the *last* ten verses.
- Imam Ahmad recorded from al-Barāʼ the story of a man who was reciting al-Kahf when an animal in the house grew nervous, and he saw a fog or cloud overhead. The Prophet ﷺ told him: "Keep on reciting, for this is the tranquillity (sakīnah) which descends when one reads Qurʼān, or because of reading Qurʼān." Ibn Kathir notes this is also in the Two Sahihs, and that the reciter was Usayd bin al-Hudayr.
- In his Mustadrak, al-Hakim recorded from Abu Saʿīd that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever recites Sūrat al-Kahf on Friday, it will illuminate him with light from one Friday to the next" — al-Hakim judging its chain sahih though al-Bukhari and Muslim did not record it. Al-Bayhaqi also recorded in his Sunan that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever recites Sūrat al-Kahf as it was revealed, it will be a light for him on the Day of Resurrection." (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that a related Friday report — mentioning forgiveness between one Jumuʿah and the next — was declared by Ibn Kathir to be *mawqūf*, meaning its narration stops at a Companion rather than ascending to the Prophet ﷺ.)
- The Musnad of Ahmad reports from Sahl ibn Muʿādh that the Prophet ﷺ said: "One who recites the first and the last verses of Sūrah al-Kahf, for him there is light from his feet up to his head. And the one who were to recite the whole sūrah, then for him there is light from the earth up to the sky."
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites, via Hafiz Diyāʼ al-Maqdisi's Al-Mukhtārah from ʿAli, that reciting al-Kahf on Friday protects from every fitnah (trial), including the trials of the Dajjal should he appear; and a report from Dailami on the authority of Anas, cited in Rūh al-Maʿānī, that the entire sūrah was revealed at one time accompanied by seventy thousand angels — a sign of its majesty.

## Living these ayat

The passage's own demands are concrete. Ayah 2 defines the believer it congratulates: one who believes *and does righteous deeds* — so let faith show in action. The occasion of revelation teaches the habit the sūrah itself will command: never promise "tomorrow" without saying *inshāʼ Allāh*. And the Sunnah attaches a simple, achievable practice to these very lines: memorize the opening ayat of al-Kahf, and make its recitation part of your Friday — a light from one Jumuʿah to the next, and, by Allah's leave, a protection from the Dajjal and his trials, as the reports above describe.

passages.title: Consoling the Prophet; the earth as a test
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are Allah's tender address to His Messenger ﷺ at a moment of real anguish: do not let grief over those who refuse to believe consume you — and here is why their refusal, and this whole glittering world they cling to, must be seen for what it is. What binds the passage together is a single movement of thought: from the Prophet's ﷺ sorrow (ayah 6), to the adorned world in which people are tested (ayah 7), to the end of that world itself (ayah 8). The consolation is not merely "do not be sad"; it is a complete re-framing of what this earth is — a decorated testing-ground that will one day be stripped bare.

## A grief that could kill

The wording of ayah 6 is startling. *Bākhiʿun nafsak* — "perhaps you will kill yourself in grief" — describes not ordinary sadness but a sorrow so intense it threatens to destroy the one who carries it. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is here consoling His Messenger ﷺ for his sorrow over the idolaters — that they would not believe and kept away from him — and that "this narration" (*hādhā al-ḥadīth*) which they rejected means the Qur'an itself.

Ibn Kathir shows that this is not an isolated verse but a recurring divine consolation. He sets it beside its sister ayat: "So destroy not yourself in sorrow for them" (35:8), "And grieve not over them" (16:127), and "It may be that you are going to kill yourself with grief, that they do not become believers" (26:3) — again and again, revelation returns to the same reassurance.

On the word *asafan* ("in grief") at the end of the ayah, Ibn Kathir records the early commentators: Qatadah said it means "killing yourself with anger and grief over them," and Mujahid said "with anxiety." Ibn Kathir notes these are synonymous, and draws out the meaning: do not feel sorry for them — just convey the Message of Allah. Whoever goes the right way goes right only for his own benefit, and whoever goes astray strays only at his own loss. The Prophet's ﷺ duty was delivery of the message, not the production of faith in hearts; that belongs to Allah alone.

## The occasion of revelation

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Imam Ibn Jarir al-Tabari from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas, relates the occasion behind the revelation of this surah. The Quraysh of Makkah, disturbed by the Prophet's ﷺ rising influence, sent Nadr ibn Harith and ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt to the Jewish scholars of Madinah, learned in the earlier scriptures. Those scholars gave them three test questions: ask him about the young men who left their city in the distant past (a unique event), about the man who travelled the East and West of the earth, and about the Rūḥ (the soul). If he answers rightly, he is a Prophet; if not, a pretender.

The emissaries returned, the questions were put to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said he would answer them tomorrow — but forgot to say *inshā' Allāh* ("if Allah wills"). No revelation came the next day. Fifteen days passed with no Jibra'il and no revelation, and the Quraysh began throwing taunts that caused the Prophet ﷺ real pain. Then Jibra'il came with Surah al-Kahf — containing the story of the People of the Cave, the travels of Dhul-Qarnayn, and, within the surah itself, the explanation of the delay: one should say *inshā' Allāh* when promising anything of the future (a point taken up at 18:23–24). The commentators present this account as the background of the surah as a whole; the grief that ayah 6 itself addresses, as Ibn Kathir explains it, is the Prophet's ﷺ sorrow that the idolaters would not believe.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also records the special standing of this surah's opening: according to a narration of Abu al-Darda' appearing in Muslim, Abu Dawud, Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and the Musnad of Ahmad, one who has memorized the first ten verses of Surah al-Kahf — the very verses we are reading — will remain protected from the ill effects of Dajjal (imposter). In another report in the same books and from the same authority, the same thing is said of memorizing the surah's last ten verses.

## Why the world glitters: ayah 7

Having consoled His Messenger ﷺ, Allah turns to explain the deeper reality behind the world people cling to. Ibn Kathir writes that Allah made this world a temporary abode, adorned with transient beauty — a place of trial, not a place of settlement. The adornment is deliberate, and so is its purpose: "in order that We may test which of them are best in deeds."

Ibn Kathir records here a hadith narrated through Abu Maslamah, from Abu Nadrah, from Abu Saʿid, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "This world is sweet and green, and Allah makes you generations succeeding one another, so He is watching what you will do. Beware of (the beguilements of) this world and beware of women, for the first affliction that the Children of Israel suffered from was that of women." The hadith reads almost as a commentary on the ayah: the sweetness and greenness are real, the succession of generations is real, and over it all — Allah is watching what you will do.

**Even the scorpions are adornment.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises a sharp question on this verse. The ayah says Allah made "whatever is on the earth" an adornment for it — all living forms, vegetation, mountains, minerals, everything. But the earth also contains snakes, scorpions, beasts, and many harmful and fatal things; how can these be called adornment? The answer given: the doubt is unfounded, because a thing may be harmful in a restricted sense while, in terms of the totality of creation, nothing is bad. Everything, however dangerous, has been invested by Allah with benefits on other counts — the medical use of poisonous creatures in the service of human beings is one example. Judged by the function of the entire universe, even the "bad" things belong to its beauty.

## And then, bare ground: ayah 8

The passage closes by pulling the curtain back on where all this adornment is heading. *Ṣaʿīdan juruzan* — bare, dry soil. Ibn Kathir explains: after having adorned it, Allah will destroy it and make everything on it bare and dry, with no vegetation or any other benefit. He gathers the words of the early authorities: al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that everything on it will be wiped out and destroyed; Mujahid said "a dry and barren plain"; Qatadah said, "a plain on which there are no trees or vegetation."

The sequence of the three ayat is itself the consolation. Why grieve to death over people who reject the Qur'an? Because what they have chosen instead — the sweet, green, decorated earth — was only ever stage-scenery for a test, and the stage itself will be stripped to dust. Their refusal loses them everything; it takes nothing from the message or its bearer.

## Living it

Two practical threads run through the passage as the commentators present it. First, for anyone who calls others to truth — a parent, a teacher, a daʿwah worker: your responsibility, as Ibn Kathir puts it, is to convey the Message of Allah; guidance and misguidance fall to the benefit or loss of the hearer alone. Care deeply, but do not let another person's rejection destroy you. Second, the believer is meant to walk through this adorned world with the Prophet's ﷺ words in mind — it is sweet and green, and Allah is watching what you will do. The adornment is not a trap to flee nor a home to settle in; it is the material of the exam, and the exam is *aḥsanu ʿamalan* — who is best in deeds.

passages.title: The people of the cave introduced in summary
passages.tafsir:
## The whole story in four ayat

These four ayat are the Qur'an's own summary of the story of the People of the Cave: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah first tells the story "in brief and general terms, then He explains it in more detail." Ayah 9 poses a question that reframes how we should see the miracle; ayah 10 gives us the young men and their prayer; ayah 11 the long miraculous sleep; ayah 12 the awakening and its purpose. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it at the close of its discussion: up to this point the Qur'an has mentioned the story in brief — details follow.

## Ayah 9: Is this really the greatest wonder?

The passage opens with a gentle challenge to the Prophet ﷺ — and through him, to everyone who found this story astonishing: *"Do you think that the people of al-Kahf and ar-Raqim were a wonder among Our signs?"*

Ibn Kathir unpacks the point: their case was not something amazing compared to Allah's power. The creation of the heavens and the earth, the alternation of night and day, the subjugation of the sun, moon and heavenly bodies — these are mightier signs, and the One who does all that is not incapable of things more amazing than the story of the people of the Cave. Mujahid put it simply: "Among Our signs are things that are more amazing than this." Ibn 'Abbas gave the thought a striking turn: what Allah has given you of knowledge, the Sunnah and the Book is *far better* than the story of the People of al-Kahf and ar-Raqim. In other words: the Qur'an in your hands is a greater marvel than the sleepers you are asking about. Muhammad bin Ishaq read the ayah the other way — "I have not shown My creatures a proof more amazing than this story" — but both readings converge on the same lesson: the story is a sign pointing to Allah's power, not a curiosity to gawk at.

## Two names: al-Kahf and ar-Raqim

**Al-Kahf.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the precision of the word: *kahf* is a *large* mountain cave; a small one would be a *ghār*. The Qur'an is already telling us something about the place.

**Ar-Raqim.** This word occupied the early scholars, because it literally means *al-marqūm* — "something written." The views Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmit include:

- **A written tablet** — Sa'id bin Jubayr said it was a stone tablet on which the story of the sleepers was written and placed at the cave's entrance. Ad-Dahhak, as-Suddi and Ibn Jubayr, on the authority of Ibn 'Abbas, said the ruler of the time had the youths' names inscribed on it and fixed it at the entrance — hence they are also called the People of al-Raqim, "the inscribed ones."
- **The valley** — Qatadah, 'Atiyyah al-'Awfi and Mujahid (in one report) said Raqim is the valley adjoining the mountain of the cave; a narration from Ibn 'Abbas places the valley near Aylah — that is, 'Aqabah.
- **The mountain, the town, or their buildings** — other reports from Ibn 'Abbas, Ka'b and Mujahid.

Ibn 'Abbas himself was heard by 'Ikrimah to say, "I do not know whether Raqim is the name of some inscribed tablet or some town" — a companion of his rank comfortable saying *I don't know* about a Qur'anic word is itself a lesson in scholarly honesty.

**One group or two?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records a subtle discussion here. Imam al-Bukhari, in his Sahih, gave two separate chapter headings — Ashab al-Kahf and Ashab al-Raqim — and under the latter placed the well-known story of three men shut into a cave by a fallen rock, who were released when each supplicated by a righteous deed he had done for Allah's good pleasure. This arrangement suggests he considered them two separate groups. But Hafiz Ibn Hajar, the commentator of al-Bukhari, examined the evidence and concluded otherwise: the sentence connecting the Prophet's ﷺ mention of Raqim to the story of those three men appears only in an addition found in the reports of al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani, not in the reports found in the six Sahihs, nor even in al-Bukhari's own version — and even that sentence does not clearly say the Prophet ﷺ *named* the three men the People of Raqim. Moreover, the very fact that the Companions and their successors differed so widely about the meaning of Raqim is itself proof that the Prophet ﷺ left no definitive statement about it. Ibn Hajar therefore held that the People of the Cave and the People of ar-Raqim are one single group, and the majority of commentators and hadith experts agree that they both are one and the same.

## Ayah 10: young men, and a prayer worth memorising

*"When the young men took refuge in the cave..."* The word is *fityah*, plural of *fatā* — a young man. These were youths who fled from their people for the sake of their religion, fearing persecution, and hid in a mountain cave. And the very first thing the Qur'an records of them inside the cave is not a plan but a prayer:

*"Our Lord! Bestow on us mercy from Yourself, and facilitate for us our affair in the right way (rashadā)."*

Ibn Kathir opens up both halves. "Mercy *from Yourself*" — *min ladunka* — means: give us Your mercy and conceal us from our people. And "facilitate our affair in the right way" means: direct our matter well — grant us a *good end*. Ibn Kathir notes this is as was reported in the Hadith: "Whatever You have decreed for us, make its consequences good." They did not ask to be spared hardship; they asked that whatever Allah had decreed for them end well.

## Ayah 11: what "We struck upon their ears" means

The Arabic of ayah 11 is an idiom worth savouring: *fa-darabnā ʿalā ādhānihim* — literally, "We struck upon their ears," i.e. veiled their hearing. Ibn Kathir explains it plainly: We caused them to sleep when they entered the cave, and they slept for many years. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *why the ear* is singled out: when a person falls asleep, the eyes close first while the ears stay active — sounds are still heard. Only when sleep takes over completely do the ears stop functioning. And when a sleeper wakes, it is the ears that resume first — a sound startles him out of his sleep. So sealing the *ears* describes the deepest possible sleep, lasting "a number of years" — left uncounted here.

## Ayah 12: awakened for a purpose

*"Then We raised them up, that We might test which of the two parties was best at calculating the time period they tarried."* Ibn Kathir explains that the "two parties" are those who disputed about the sleepers; it was said that what they disputed was how long the youths had stayed in the cave. And he notes what the awakening looked like: one of them went out with his dirhams (silver coins) to buy food — a detail the sūrah will discuss in more detail later.

## The story behind the summary

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān transmits the fuller background in the brief version Ibn Kathir presented with reference to many early and later commentators. The youths were the progeny of kings and chiefs among an idol-worshipping people ruled by a tyrant called Daqyanus, who forced idol-worship on his subjects. At an annual festival where the people worshipped their idols and sacrificed animals to them, Allah blessed each of these young men with the good sense to see that worship belongs only to the supreme Power who created the heavens and the earth and everything therein. The thought crossed their minds simultaneously, yet each withdrew from the crowd on his own and sat under the same tree, strangers to one another. Ibn Kathir pauses here with a profound observation: people credit nationalism and shared race with binding societies together, but the reality lies in what has been said in a Hadith of Sahih al-Bukhari — that unity or disunity first germinates in souls, and only then affects the bodies in this world. Souls that experienced congruity in eternity become connected in this world. Here was the proof: one conviction, arising in separate hearts, gathered strangers under one tree.

At first each concealed his belief, fearing betrayal to the king. Then one spoke — "brothers, there must be some reason why all of us have broken away from our people and reached here" — and the truth came out: every one of them had rejected the idols for the One Lord. Now an ideologically unified brotherhood, they set up a house of worship and worshipped Allah alone, until word reached Daqyanus. Summoned to court, Allah gave them the courage not merely to state their belief but to invite the king himself to it. This, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, is precisely what is mentioned in the verses appearing next in the sūrah: "And We made their hearts firm. And when they rose, they said, 'Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth'" (al-Kahf, 18:14–15). The king stripped them of their princely robes and gave them a few days' respite to recant, on pain of death. That respite, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, must have been Allah's mercy opening an escape door for them: they ran and took refuge in a cave — the moment ayah 10 captures.

Most commentators hold these youths were followers of the faith of 'Isa عليه السلام — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Ibn Ishaq's report in Tafsir Mazhari, describes them as rare monotheist remnants still adhering to the true faith after the original Christian faith declined, living in the city of Ifsus (Ephesus). Ibn Kathir himself did not accept this, arguing the Jews of Madinah would not have proposed a test-question about followers of the Christian faith; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers that the Jews asked simply because it was a unique event, just as they asked about Dhul-Qarnayn.

## What Allah left unstated — leave it unstated

Where exactly was the cave? Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān record candidate sites — near Aylah/'Aqabah (favoured by most narrations from Ibn 'Abbas), Ifsus (Ephesus) in Asia Minor (favoured by nearly all the tafsir reports of al-Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Jarir), even a cave near Granada in Spain that Ibn 'Atiyyah personally visited in 504 AH, and a cave excavated near Amman in 1963. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's verdict on all of it: no categorical decision is possible, and none is needed. The Companions and Successors laid down the principle, recorded in al-Itqan of al-Suyuti: **"What Allah has left undetermined, you too leave it undetermined."** The Qur'an, with the sole exception of the story of Yusuf عليه السلام, never narrates a story in full historical order; it gives only the parts that guide and teach. Ibn Kathir says it perfectly: Allah told us of the event and expects us to understand and deliberate on it — but He did not tell us in which land the cave lies, "because there is nothing beneficial for us in it nor does any religious objective hinge upon it."

A remarkable incident drives this home. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates (via Ruh al-Ma'ani) that during a campaign against Byzantine forces, Mu'awiyah رضي الله عنه passed the site said to be the cave and wished to enter and see the sleepers. Ibn 'Abbas رضي الله عنه counselled against it: Allah had already prohibited someone better than you from seeing them — the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — for the Qur'an says, "If you had a look at them, you would have fled away from them and would have been filled with awe of them" (ayah 18 of this sūrah). Men were sent anyway; a punishing wind drove them out of the cave. And are the sleepers alive today? The correct and obvious position, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is that they have died — and Ibn 'Abbas, passing a cave in the Roman territory where bones were claimed to be theirs, replied that their bones had become dust more than three hundred years before.

## Living it

Three things this summary passage asks of a believer. **First**, when faith is threatened, flight to protect it is not weakness — these youths fled their people for the sake of their religion, and the Qur'an honours them for it. **Second**, their first act in the cave is the believer's template in every refuge: ask Allah for mercy from Himself, and for *rashad* — that whatever He has decreed end well. **Third**, receive the Qur'an's stories the way the Qur'an tells them: take the guidance, marvel at the sign, and entrust to Allah the details He deliberately veiled.

passages.title: The youths' faith, retreat, and miraculous sleep
passages.tafsir:
# The Youths of the Cave: Faith, Flight, and the Sleep That Was a Sign

With ayah 13 the surah turns from its brief preview of the story of the Cave to the story itself: "We relate to you their story in truth." What holds ayat 13–20 together is a single arc — a handful of young men come to faith, stand up for it before a tyrant, flee with their religion to a cave, and are placed by Allah into a miraculous centuries-long sleep from which He then wakes them. Ibn Kathir reads the whole passage as Allah Himself now explaining the story in detail, and every scene in it — the firm hearts, the sheltering cave, the angled sunlight, the turning bodies, the confused awakening — is presented as a sign (ayah) of Allah's power and care for those who hold to His oneness.

## "They were young men" — why their youth matters

The first thing Allah tells us about them, in ayah 13, is their age: *fityah*, the plural of *fata*, a young man. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the Tafsir scholars drew a lesson from this very word: the time ripe for the correction of deeds and character, and for taking on guidance, is invariably youth. Once a person grows old, acquired habits and beliefs become so deeply rooted that even when the truth is plain, it is very hard to break free of them. Ibn Kathir makes the same point historically: these youths were more accepting of the truth and more guided than their elders, who had become stubbornly set in the religion of falsehood — just as most of those who responded to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ were young people, while most of the elders of Quraysh clung to their religion and only a few embraced Islam. Mujahid even relates that some of these youths had worn earrings — ordinary young men of their society — before Allah guided them, inspired them to fear Him, and led them to bear witness that there is no god besides Him.

Ayah 13 then adds: "and We increased them in guidance." Ibn Kathir records that from this ayah and others like it — such as 47:17, 9:124 and 48:4 — several scholars, including al-Bukhari, understood a point of creed: faith can increase, vary in degrees, and fluctuate. Guidance is not a fixed quantity given once; Allah adds to it for those who act on it.

Who were they, historically? Ibn Kathir mentions the view that they followed the religion of ʿIsa ibn Maryam, but he himself inclines to the view that they lived before Christianity altogether — because the Jewish rabbis of Madinah were the ones who told Quraysh to test the Prophet ﷺ by asking about these young men (along with Dhul-Qarnayn and the Ruh), and the rabbis would not have cared to preserve a Christian story. The story, he concludes, was recorded in the books of the People of the Book from before that era — and Allah knows best.

## Ayah 14: hearts tied firm before a king

"And We strengthened their hearts (*wa-rabatna ʿala qulubihim*) when they stood up and said: Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." Ibn Kathir explains the strengthening: Allah gave them the patience to go against their own people and city, and to walk away from the life of luxury and ease they had been living — for several earlier and later Tafsir scholars relate that they were sons of the kings and leaders of Byzantium.

The story behind this ayah, as Ibn Kathir tells it, is worth telling properly. Their people held an annual festival outside the city, gathering to worship idols and offer sacrifices, urged on by an arrogant, tyrannical king called Decianus. These young men went out with their fathers — and, seeing the scene with clear insight, each of them realized independently that prostration and sacrifice belong only to Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth. Each quietly began to withdraw. One went and sat in the shade of a tree; another came and sat with him; then another; then four more, one by one. None of them knew the others — "they were brought together," Ibn Kathir says, "by the One Who instilled faith in their hearts." He cites here the hadith recorded by al-Bukhari (with an incomplete chain) from ʿA'ishah, and by Muslim in his Sahih from Abu Hurayrah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Souls are like recruited soldiers: those that recognize one another come together, and those that do not recognize one another turn away from each other."

At first each concealed his belief from the others out of fear. Then one of them said: only one thing can have made all of you leave your people — let each man say what it is. One confessed: "By Allah, I saw what my people are doing and realized it was false; the only One Who deserves worship, alone and without partner, is Allah Who created everything." The others said the same, and they became brothers in faith, taking a place where they worshipped Allah — until their people found out and reported them to the king.

This is the moment ayah 14 describes. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says plainly: when the cruel, idol-worshipping king summoned them to his court and questioned them, it was a matter of life and death. Yet despite their fear of the worst, Allah made His love, awe and grandeur prevail over their hearts, and they proclaimed their belief clearly and courageously — they worshipped no one but Allah and never would. Maʿārif draws the general rule: those who firmly resolve to act for the sake of Allah receive help from Allah in exactly this way.

Notice the language of their declaration. They said *lan nadʿuwa* — "never shall we call upon any god other than Him." Ibn Kathir points out that *lan* implies an absolute, eternal negation: this will never happen. And they added: "if we did, we would have uttered *shatat*" — an enormity, an utter falsehood.

## Ayah 15: turning the burden of proof

In ayah 15 the youths reason with each other about their people: "These people of ours have taken gods besides Him — why do they not bring for them a clear authority (*sultan bayyin*)?" Ibn Kathir explains: why do they not produce some clear evidence and genuine proof for what they do? Worship of anything besides Allah rests on no proof at all — and so, the ayah concludes, "who does more wrong than he who invents a lie against Allah?" Idolatry is not merely an error; it is a fabrication against Allah, and there is no wrong greater.

## Ayah 16: fleeing with one's religion

The king, refusing their call to Allah, threatened them, had them stripped of the adorned clothing of their people, and gave them time to reconsider — hoping they would revert. Ibn Kathir sees Allah's kindness precisely in that delay: it gave them the window to escape. Ayah 16 records their resolve to one another: "Since you have withdrawn from them and from what they worship besides Allah, take refuge in the cave; your Lord will spread out for you something of His mercy and make easy for you your affair." Ibn Kathir unpacks the sequence: you have already separated from them in religion — now separate from them physically too. Allah's mercy will conceal you from your people, and He will provide what you need (*mirfaq* — ease, provision for their affair).

Ibn Kathir then states the ruling this models: in times of trial and persecution, a person who fears for his religion is prescribed to flee from his persecutors — citing the hadith that a time will come when the best wealth a man can have will be sheep he follows to the mountaintops and the places of rainfall, fleeing with his religion from tribulation. But he immediately fences the ruling: seclusion from people is allowed in such cases only, not otherwise, because seclusion costs a person the congregational and Friday prayers. On this ayah Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same lesson in Ibn Kathir's name: Ibn Kathir says that the course the People of the Cave adopted — leaving a city in which Allah could not be worshipped and taking refuge where worship was possible — is the Sunnah, the way, of all the prophets, who migrate from such places to a place where ʿibadah can be done.

Ibn Kathir closes this scene with a moving parallel. When the king searched for the vanished youths, Allah concealed them so completely that no trace could be found — just as Allah concealed His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and Abu Bakr as-Siddiq in the cave of Thawr, when the pursuing Quraysh passed right by them. When Abu Bakr said, "O Messenger of Allah, if one of them looks down at his feet he will see us," the Prophet ﷺ replied: "O Abu Bakr, what do you think of two who have Allah as their third?" And Allah revealed of that moment: "Do not grieve; surely Allah is with us" (9:40). Ibn Kathir remarks: the story of that cave is far greater and more wondrous than the story of the People of the Cave.

## Ayah 17: the sun that turned aside

Ayah 17 zooms in on the cave itself: the rising sun inclining away to the right, the setting sun passing them on the left, while they lay in an open space within — "that is from the signs of Allah." Ibn Kathir, reasoning from the sun's path, deduces that the cave's entrance faced north, explaining in detail why an east-, south-, or west-facing entrance would not match the description; Ibn ʿAbbas held that the sunlight entered the cave without ever touching them, for direct sun over centuries would have burnt their bodies and clothes. Yet Ibn Kathir also notes what Allah deliberately withheld: the cave's location. Allah described its features but not its place, because knowing it serves no religious benefit — had it done so, Allah and His Messenger ﷺ would have taught it to us, as the Prophet ﷺ said he left nothing that brings us nearer to Paradise and further from the Fire without teaching it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames ayat 17–18 as describing wonders (*karamah*) surrounding these devoted servants — explaining the terminology: a wonder manifested at the hands of a prophet is a *muʿjizah* (miracle), while one appearing at the hands of other pious people is a *karamah*. On how the sun was kept off them, the scholars genuinely differed: Ibn Qutaibah made elaborate calculations to fix the cave's peculiar orientation, treating it as natural positioning; al-Zajjaj held it was not the cave's formation at all but an extraordinary karamah — and al-Qurtubi observed that the closing words "that is from the signs of Allah" support the latter reading. Maʿārif's own balanced conclusion: Allah arranged their protection — whether through the cave's formation, some barrier, or the rays themselves being turned aside — all these possibilities sit within the ayah, and there is no need to insist on fixing one as the absolute reality.

## Ayah 18: asleep, yet you would think them awake

Three strange mercies fill ayah 18. First, "you would have thought them awake, though they were asleep." Scholars mention that their eyelids did not close — open eyes exposed to the air were better for preservation, Ibn Kathir relates — and Maʿārif adds that none of the ordinary marks of sleep were on them: no slackness of the body, no changed rhythm of breath. The wisdom, Maʿārif suggests, was protective: no one would attack or rob men who seemed awake.

Second, "We turned them on their right and on their left sides." Ibn ʿAbbas said: had they not been turned, the earth would have consumed them.

Third, "their dog stretching out its forelegs at the threshold (*wasid*)" — the threshold or doorway, as Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Saʿid ibn Jubayr and Qatadah explained. The dog lay at the door as dogs do — Ibn Jurayj said, guarding it — and remained outside, Ibn Kathir notes, because angels do not enter a house in which there is a dog, as reported in the Sahih. Maʿārif raises the obvious question: given the hadith in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from Ibn ʿUmar that whoever keeps a dog other than for hunting or guarding livestock loses two qirats of reward daily, why did these righteous men have a dog? Perhaps, it answers, that prohibition belongs to the Shariʿah of Muhammad ﷺ and was not part of the earlier law; and men of property may well have kept a guard dog which faithfully followed them out of the city.

Then comes one of the most beloved lessons of the whole story. The sleep that blessed the youths overtook their dog too. "This," writes Ibn Kathir, "is the benefit of accompanying good people" — the dog attained fame and stature by their company. Maʿārif relates how this lesson was once preached: Ibn ʿAtiyyah says that his father told him he heard a sermon of Abu al-Fadl Jawhari, delivered in the year 469 AH at the Great Mosque of Egypt, in which the preacher told the people that whoever loves good people gets a share of their goodness — see how, when the dog of the People of the Cave loved them and kept close to them, Allah mentioned it in the Qur'an. Al-Qurtubi records this report of Ibn ʿAtiyyah in his Tafsir and adds his own comment: if a dog can reach such a station by keeping company with the righteous, imagine the station of true believers and pure monotheists who love the righteous servants of Allah — and there is comfort here for Muslims weak in deeds who sincerely love the Prophet ﷺ. Maʿārif seals the point with the hadith in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from Anas: a man asked the Prophet ﷺ when the Hour would come; he asked what the man had prepared for it; the man said he had not amassed much prayer, fasting or charity, "but I love Allah and His Messenger" — and the Prophet ﷺ said: "You shall be with those whom you love." Anas said the Companions had never rejoiced at anything as they rejoiced at that sentence.

Finally, ayah 18 says that had you come upon them, you would have fled in terror, filled with awe. Allah cast this dread over them, Ibn Kathir explains, precisely so that no one would approach or touch them before the appointed time. As to the basis of the awe, Maʿārif counsels restraint: the Qur'an and hadith did not explain it, so conjecture is futile — it may have worked through physical causes or as pure karamah. It relates the report (cited via Tafsir Mazhari from Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim) that on a campaign against Byzantium, Muʿawiyah wished to enter the cave and see the bodies. Ibn ʿAbbas objected, reciting this very ayah — Allah had withheld the sight from one better than you, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — showing that in Ibn ʿAbbas's reading the address "had you looked upon them" was to the Prophet ﷺ himself, while Muʿawiyah apparently took it as addressed to people generally. Muʿawiyah sent men anyway; a hot wind was sent upon them and they could see nothing.

## Ayat 19–20: the awakening

"And likewise (*kadhalika*) We awakened them, so that they might question one another." Maʿārif dwells on that opening word: the raising was *like* the sleep — just as their sleep was no ordinary sleep, their rising after hundreds of years, intact, healthy and fit without any nourishment, was equally a sign of Allah's power. Ibn Kathir: Allah resurrected them with bodies, hair and skin intact, unchanged in form — after three hundred and nine years. And the *lam* in "so that they might question one another" is, the grammarians say (Abu Hayyan, al-Qurtubi), the lam of consequence: the questioning was the natural sequel of the awakening — and, Maʿārif adds, the beginning of the process by which their city would in time come to know of them.

Their exchange is touchingly human. "How long have you stayed?" "A day, or part of a day" — for they had entered the cave in the morning and awoke in the evening. But some of them sensed that this might not be the same day at all, and closed the debate with the words believers should always be ready to say: "Your Lord knows best how long you have stayed." Maʿārif praises this move — they dismissed an unresolvable dispute and turned to the need of the hour: food.

"So send one of you with this silver coin of yours to the city." Ibn Kathir notes they had brought dirhams from home, had given some in charity and kept some; Maʿārif deduces from this that carrying provision and managing one's necessary expenses does not contradict *zuhd* (detachment from the world) or *tawakkul* (trust in Allah). The definite "the city" shows they meant their known home city — which Abu Hayyan names as Ifsus, later renamed Tarsus; al-Qurtubi explains that it was called Ifsus in its days of idol-worship, and was renamed Tarsus when the believing followers of ʿIsa later overtook it.

They ask the messenger to find which food is *azka* — "purest." Ibn Kathir connects the root to zakah itself, the purification of wealth. By the tafsir of Saʿid ibn Jubayr, it means halal food: when they left the city, animals were slaughtered in the names of idols and sold in the market, so they insisted on verification first. Maʿārif derives the ruling: in a place where most available food is haram, one may not eat without prior investigation. Al-Qurtubi (via Ibn Khuwaizmandad) draws further rulings from "send one of you with this silver of yours": shared capital (partnership) is permissible; so is agency — one person disbursing from shared wealth with the others' permission; and so is a group sharing food though individuals eat unequal amounts.

"And let him be careful, and let no one know of you" (19), "for if they discover you, they will stone you or force you back into their religion — and then you would never succeed" (20). *Rajm* means stoning to death — Maʿārif notes it was their people's public, collective punishment for one who abandoned their religion, everyone joining in. And the youths' final sentence states the stake with perfect clarity, as Ibn Kathir explains: to return to that religion, even under torture by the followers of Decianus, would mean never attaining success — not in this world and not in the Hereafter.

## What the passage leaves with us

Read as one unit, ayat 13–20 trace the full anatomy of faith under persecution: conviction that arrives in youth and is increased by Allah; hearts tied firm to speak the truth before power; the prescribed flight when religion itself is in danger; and then Allah's answer to their trust — mercy spread out for them, their bodies guarded by angled sunlight, turning sides, a watchdog, and a God-given awe, until the day He woke them as a sign. They asked only for refuge in a cave; Allah made them a sign for all who would ever flee to Him.

passages.title: Discovery, disputes, and saying 'if Allah wills'
passages.tafsir:
# The Sleepers Discovered: Signs, Disputes, and the Etiquette of "If Allah Wills"

This passage closes the story of the People of the Cave. Ayah 21 tells how Allah caused the sleepers to be discovered — and why: so that a doubting generation would see with their own eyes that His promise of resurrection is true. What follows flows naturally from that discovery: the disputes it provoked — over what to build at the cave (ayah 21), over how many sleepers there were (ayah 22), over how long they slept (ayat 25–26) — and, set in the middle of it all, a piece of prophetic training that arose from this very sūrah's revelation: never to speak of tomorrow without saying "if Allah wills" (ayat 23–24). What holds the passage together is a single thread: real knowledge of the unseen belongs to Allah alone, and the believer's speech — about the future, about hidden matters, about disputed details — must reflect that.

## How the secret came out

Ayah 21 opens: "That is how We caused them to be discovered, so that they might know that the promise of Allah is true, and that there is no doubt about the Hour." Ibn Kathir explains the word *aʿtharnā* simply: "We caused the people to find them." Just as Allah had put them to sleep and then woken them physically intact, He now made their story known — deliberately, and with perfect timing.

Several scholars of the Salaf, Ibn Kathir reports, mentioned that the people of that later era were skeptical about the Resurrection. ʿIkrimah said a group among them held that souls would be resurrected but not bodies — so Allah resurrected the People of the Cave as a sign and proof.

Ibn Kathir then relates the story of the discovery as it was passed down. The sleepers wanted to send one of their number to the city — which, in this account, was called Daqsus — to buy food. He disguised himself and set out by a different route, thinking little time had passed; in fact century after century had gone by, and the country and its people had changed. He recognized no landmark and no face, elite or commoner. He began to wonder: "Maybe I am crazy or deluded, maybe I am dreaming" — then steadied himself: "By Allah, I am nothing of the sort; what I know I saw last night was different from this." He went to a man selling food and offered him his money. The seller did not recognize the coin or its imprint, passed it to his neighbor, and soon the traders were passing it around, saying, "Maybe this man found some treasure." They asked him who he was and where the money came from. He said, "I am from this land, I was living here yesterday and Decianus was the ruler." They accused him of being crazy and took him to the governor, who questioned him; then the king and the people of the city went with him to the cave, where he asked to go in first and tell his companions. Here the reports diverge: it was said that the people never learned how he entered, and never learned the sleepers' story; and it was also said that they did enter and see them, and that the king — apparently a Muslim, whose name in this account was Tedosis — greeted and embraced them. They rejoiced at meeting him and spoke with him, then bid him farewell, returned to their sleep, and Allah caused them to die. Ibn Kathir closes as the reports themselves do: and Allah knows best.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a parallel telling, summarized from Tafsir al-Qurtubi, in which the incidental details — and even the names — differ. In this account, the persecuting Mushrik king was Daqyanus; after the youths fled, he died, and centuries went by. The city was eventually taken over by pure monotheists, whose king was a righteous man (named Baidusis in Tafsir Mazhari, with reference to historical narratives). In his time, dispute raged over whether decomposed bodies could rise again on the Day of Qiyamah. When nothing the king tried worked, he put on ragged clothes, sat on a heap of ash, and pleaded with Allah to set his people's belief right. On the other side of the city, Allah arranged the answer to his prayer in His own way: the sleepers awoke and sent one of their men (reportedly named Tamlikha) to the bazaar to buy food. He paid with a silver coin dating back to the time of Daqyanus, who had reigned three hundred years earlier. The astonished shopkeepers passed it around — surely the man had struck some treasure — then detained him and produced him before the king. This king, the account says, already knew something of the story: reports mention an inscribed tablet preserving the names of the youths who had fled Daqyanus for their faith (the tablet was called *Raqīm*, which is why the sleepers were also known as the People of Raqīm). When the king inquired into Tamlikha's background, he was convinced this was one of the People of the Cave — and that Allah had heard his prayer. He asked to be taken to the cave and arrived with a retinue of citizens. Tamlikha went in first, to reassure his companions that this king, unlike the last, was a believer, a monotheist, with a believing people. Most narratives in this telling say that when Tamlikha related the story, his companions died and never met the king; another report, which Abu Hayyan relates in al-Bahr al-Muhit, says they greeted the king, then returned into the cave, where Allah sent death upon them. The two tellings, then, agree on the substance and differ on details the sources make no attempt to reconcile; the commentators end each of them the only way such reports can end — Allah knows best the reality as it is.

The lesson the city drew is the lesson the ayah names. They had seen human beings kept alive three hundred years without food, then raised intact and healthy. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, their assumption that bodily resurrection was far-fetched stood refuted; they realized that measuring the power of the Master of the universes by the yardstick of human power was itself an act of ignorance. Some in the city had believed in resurrection and some had denied it — so Allah made this discovery evidence, in Ibn Kathir's words, "either in their favor or against them."

## The building over the cave — and a caution from the Sunnah

The end of ayah 21 records what happened next: some said, "Construct a building over them; their Lord knows best about them," while "those who won their point" said, "We shall surely build over them a place of worship (masjid)." Ibn Kathir explains the first proposal as: seal the cave's entrance and leave them as they are. Those who prevailed were the people of power and influence — in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's account, the believing king and his officials, who wanted a mosque as a memorial and a safeguard against the idol-worship that still lingered in the city.

Were those who built the place of worship right to do so? Ibn Kathir notes that there is debate on this point, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah has cursed the Jews and the Christians who took the graves of their Prophets and righteous people as places of worship" — a warning against such practice. He adds that when ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, the Commander of the Faithful, found the grave of Danyal (Daniel) in Iraq during his rule, he ordered that news of it be withheld from the people and that the inscription found there be buried. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Mazhari, offers the reconciling ruling: building a masjid for prayer *near* the graves of the righteous is not in itself sinful; what the hadith curses is making the graves themselves an object or direction of prostration — which is, by consensus, shirk (associating partners with Allah) and forbidden.

As for the phrase "their Lord knows best about them," al-Bahr al-Muhit (as cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān) mentions two possibilities: it may be the words of the townspeople themselves, who — unable to settle the sleepers' background details for a memorial inscription — finally gave up and said, "their Lord knows them best"; or it may be Allah's own words, warning those who waste time disputing over matters they have no means of knowing — including, possibly, the Jews and others who used this story to stir up debates in the Prophet's ﷺ own time. Either way, the phrase sounds the passage's keynote.

## "Guessing at the unseen": the dispute over their number

Ayah 22 reports three claims: "three, their dog the fourth"; "five, their dog the sixth"; "seven, and their dog the eighth." The Qurʼān brands the first two *rajman bil-ghayb* — "guessing at the unseen." Ibn Kathir's image is vivid: like a person shooting at a target he cannot see — he is hardly likely to hit it, and if he does, it was not on purpose. The third opinion, by contrast, is left without censure — which, Ibn Kathir says, indicates that it is correct.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds who these disputants may have been: either the people of the sleepers' own era, or the Christians of Najran who argued with the Prophet ﷺ — their three sects each championing a number: the Malkaniyah said three, the Yaʿqubiyah five, the Nasturiyah seven (though some said the third view was that of the Muslims). The third view proved true, as the Qurʼān's hint shows.

There is also a subtle grammatical signal here, one the commentators dwell on. In the first two claims there is no "and": "three, the fourth of them their dog." But the third reads "seven, *and* the eighth of them their dog" — with the conjunction *wāw*. Commentators cited in Mazhari and elsewhere explain that the early Arabs counted up to seven as one series and treated what came after as a fresh start, marking it with a connective — hence this *wāw* became known as the "*wāw* of *thamān* (eight)." The very syntax sets the third statement apart.

Then the decisive instruction: "Say: My Lord knows best their number; none knows them but a few." Ibn Kathir draws the general rule: in matters like this, the best course is to refer knowledge to Allah — speak where you have knowledge, refrain where you do not. Yet the ayah itself concedes that a few *do* know. Qatadah reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said: "I am one of the few mentioned in this Ayah; they were seven" — and Ibn Kathir notes that the chains of these reports from Ibn ʿAbbas, recorded by Ibn Jarir, are Sahih. (As for the sleepers' *names*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is candid: they are not authentically established in any Sahih hadith; the closest is a report from Ibn ʿAbbas given by al-Tabarani in al-Muʿjam al-Awsat, listing names such as Muksalmina, Tamlikha, Martunis and others.)

The ayah ends with two commands to the Prophet ﷺ: "So do not argue about them except with an apparent (surface) argumentation, and do not ask any of them about them." Ibn Kathir reads the first as: debate only gently and politely, for there is not much to be gained; and the second as: they have no knowledge except guesswork, no evidence from an infallible source — while you, O Muhammad ﷺ, have been sent with the truth that takes priority over all previous books and sayings. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls these two sentences a golden legacy for the learned of this Ummah: when a dispute arises, state what is necessary clearly; if people insist on prolonging it, offer brief comments and close the discussion. Digging in to win the argument produces nothing good — only wasted time and the danger of mutual bitterness. And do not interrogate others either to extract more detail than revelation gave, or to expose their ignorance and humiliate them — both are beneath prophetic character.

## "If Allah wills": the lesson born of this very story

Ayat 23–24 seem, at first glance, a digression: "And never say of anything, 'I will surely do this tomorrow,' except (adding), 'if Allah wills.' And remember your Lord when you forget, and say: It may be that my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right guidance than this." But both Ibn Kathir and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān connect them directly to the occasion of this sūrah. When the Makkans — coached by the Jews — asked the Prophet ﷺ about the People of the Cave, he said, "I will tell you tomorrow," without saying *in shāʼ Allāh*. The revelation was then delayed fifteen days. The Prophet ﷺ was grieved, and the Makkan idolaters seized their chance to mock. When the answer finally came, these two verses came with it as guidance (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports this background in Lubab from Ibn ʿAbbas). As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes, even the slightest lapse from those closest to Allah draws a gentle corrective notice.

The principle, as Ibn Kathir frames it, is the correct etiquette when resolving to do anything in the future: refer it always to the will of Allah, the Knower of the Unseen, "Who knows what was and what is yet to be and what is not to be, and how it would be if it were to be." Who knows whether one will live to see tomorrow — and, living, whether one will be able to act?

Ibn Kathir then cites the striking hadith recorded in the Two Sahihs, from Abu Hurayrah: Sulayman ibn Dawud (peace be upon them both) said, "Tonight I will go around to seventy women" — ninety or a hundred in other reports — "each of whom will give birth to a son who will fight in the cause of Allah." It was said to him (in one report, by the angel), "Say: if Allah wills" — but he did not say it. None of the women bore a child except one, who gave birth to a half-formed child. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "By the One in Whose hand is my soul, had he said 'if Allah wills,' he would not have broken his oath, and it would have helped him attain what he wanted" — and in another report, "they would all have fought as horsemen in the cause of Allah." Even a prophet's resolve, unaccompanied by *in shāʼ Allāh*, does not bind the future.

**"And remember your Lord when you forget."** Abu al-ʿAliyah and al-Hasan al-Basri understood this to mean: if you forget to say "if Allah wills," say it when you remember. Ibn ʿAbbas went further: one may say it "even a year later." Ibn Kathir explains the proper sense of this — the Sunnah of saying it can still be fulfilled whenever one remembers — but he endorses Ibn Jarir's qualification: the belated saying does not undo the breaking of an oath or lift the obligation of expiation. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds the juristic ruling: saying *in shāʼ Allāh* here is *mustahabb* (recommended); it is an invocation of Allah's blessing and a confession of one's servitude — not a technical condition. Hence one should not extend this "say it when you remember" rule to sales and contracts, where a condition must be part of the agreement itself; the jurists' detailed discussions of that belong to the books of Fiqh.

The closing supplication of ayah 24 — "It may be that my Lord will guide me to something nearer to right guidance than this" — Ibn Kathir explains as: if you are asked about something you do not know, ask Allah and turn to Him, that He may guide you to what is right.

## Three hundred years, adding nine

Ayah 25 finally settles the last dispute: "And they stayed in their cave three hundred years, adding nine." Ibn Kathir explains the curious phrasing: the stay was three hundred solar years, which equals three hundred and nine lunar years — the lunar calendar gains roughly three years per century over the solar. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds why the Qurʼān expressed it this way rather than simply saying "309": the Jews and Christians reckoned by the solar calendar, so their count was three hundred; Islam reckons by the lunar calendar; the diction "three hundred… adding nine" captures both at once.

But whose statement is this? Qatadah held that "three hundred years" was the claim of the People of the Book, which Allah then refuted with "Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed" — a view also held by Mutarraf bin ʿAbdullah. Ibn Kathir respectfully rejects this: the People of the Book said three hundred *without* the nine (they counted in solar years), so if Allah were merely quoting them He would not have added "adding nine." The apparent meaning is that Allah is stating the fact — the view of Ibn Jarir, and, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the position of the majority of commentators, earlier and later, also adopted by Abu Hayyan and al-Qurtubi. On the majority reading, both sentences are Allah's word: the first states the reality; the second warns those who would still dispute it — once Allah has spoken, quarrelling with Him on the strength of conjecture is worse than unreasonable. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cautions against modernists who lean on Qatadah's view to explain the miracle away: the earlier verse "So We veiled their hearing in the Cave for a number of years" (ayah 11) is unquestionably Allah's own statement, and even that much establishes the miracle.

Notice the contrast the commentators draw. The *number* of the sleepers the Qurʼān never states outright — only a hint, by leaving the correct view unrebuked — because, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, nothing in religion or worldly life depends on it. But the *duration* is declared in plain words, because it is precisely the point of the story: a three-hundred-year sleep without food or drink, ending in a healthy awakening, is a working model of resurrection — a standing argument for the Day of Judgment.

## "How clearly He sees, and hears!"

Ayah 26 closes the story where it began — with Allah's exclusive knowledge and power: "Say: Allah knows best how long they stayed. To Him belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth." No one knows the unseen except Him, Ibn Kathir says — and whomever among His creatures He chooses to tell.

Then comes the exclamation *absir bihi wa-asmiʿ* — "How clearly He sees, and hears!" Ibn Jarir calls this "an eloquent expression of praise": how much Allah sees of all that exists, how much He hears of all that can be heard — nothing is hidden from Him. Qatadah put it simply: "No one hears or sees more than Allah."

And finally: "They have no protector besides Him, and He makes none to share in His decision and His rule." Ibn Kathir's comment is a fitting seal on the whole passage: He, may He be glorified, alone creates and commands; His ruling cannot be overturned; He has no adviser, supporter, or partner.

## Living this passage

Three habits of speech emerge from these ayat, each a form of humility before the unseen. First, when you resolve to do anything tomorrow, bind it to Allah's will — say *in shāʼ Allāh*, meaning it in the heart and on the tongue; and if you forget, say it when you remember. Second, in disputed matters where you have no real knowledge, say what the townspeople finally said and what the Prophet ﷺ was taught to say: "My Lord knows best." Speak where knowledge exists; refrain where it does not. Third, when others insist on fruitless argument, state the truth clearly, keep the exchange brief and courteous, and walk away — neither digging in to win nor questioning others to shame them. The People of the Cave were a sign that Allah's promise is true; these ayat teach us to talk like people who believe it.

passages.title: Recite the Book and stay with the sincere
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a turning point in Sūrat al-Kahf: after the story of the People of the Cave, Allah turns to address His Messenger ﷺ directly with two commands that define the believing life — hold fast to the revealed Book, and hold fast to the people who sincerely worship its Lord. What binds ayat 27–31 together is a single choice between two companies and two destinations: the company of those who remember Allah morning and evening, ending in the Gardens of ʿAdn, or the company of the heedless whose glitter ends in a wall of fire.

## The Book that cannot be changed (ayah 27)

Ibn Kathir explains that ayah 27 is Allah commanding His Messenger ﷺ to recite His Holy Book and convey it to mankind. The ayah anchors that command in a promise: *lā mubaddila li-kalimātih* — "None can change His Words." Ibn Kathir takes this to mean that no one can alter them, distort them, or misinterpret them. The Book the Prophet ﷺ is told to recite is beyond human tampering; whoever clings to it clings to something no power can corrupt.

Then comes the second half: "and none will you find as a refuge other than Him." The word is *multaḥad* — Mujahid explained it as "a shelter," and Qatadah as "a helper or supporter." Ibn Jarir drew out the force of the whole sentence: Allah is saying, "if you, O Muhammad, do not recite what is revealed to you of the Book of your Lord, then you will have no refuge from Allah." Ibn Kathir links this to the weight of the prophetic trust expressed elsewhere in the Qur'an: "O Messenger! Proclaim (the Message) which has been sent down to you from your Lord. And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His Message" (5:67), and "Verily, He Who has given you the Qur'an, will surely bring you back to the place of return" (28:85) — meaning, Ibn Kathir says, that Allah will call him to account for the duty of conveying the Message entrusted to him. Reciting and conveying the Book is not one option among many; it is the only shelter there is.

## The nobles' bargain, and Allah's refusal (ayah 28)

Ayah 28 has a story behind it, and it is the heart of this passage.

Ibn Kathir relates that it was said this ayah was revealed about the nobles of Quraysh, who asked the Prophet ﷺ to sit with them on his own and not to bring his "weak" Companions — men like Bilal, ʿAmmar, Suhayb, Khabbab, and Ibn Masʿud. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the scene with two reports, noting it is possible that all of these events together became the cause of the instruction. Al-Baghawi reports that ʿUyainah ibn Hisn al-Fazari visited the Prophet ﷺ and found Salman al-Farisi sitting there — one of the poor Companions, his dress tattered, his appearance that of a dervish — along with other poor and humble believers. ʿUyainah said: these are the people who stop us from coming to you. We cannot sit with such broken-down people. Remove them from your gathering — or at least hold one gathering for us and another for them. And Ibn Marduwayh reports from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas that Umayyah ibn Khalaf advised the Prophet ﷺ to keep the chiefs of Makkah and Quraysh close to him instead of the poor Muslims — reasoning that if the elite embraced the religion, it would advance its cause.

On the surface it sounds almost pragmatic. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious objection itself: would a separate gathering really have hurt? It might even have made it easier to bring Islam to the chiefs. The answer given is that such a division would have seated the rebellious rich on a pedestal of honor — an arrangement that could have broken the hearts of the poor Muslims or dampened their courage. Allah, in His ultimate wisdom, would not put up with anything like that. Instead He laid down what Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the ground rule of daʿwah and tabligh (calling people to Allah and conveying the message): there is to be no discrimination or distinction, against anyone or for anyone.

So the command came — and its wording is stronger than it first appears. *Waṣbir nafsaka* is usually rendered "keep yourself patiently" with them, but Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that taken literally it could mean "keep yourself **tied** to them": not merely tolerating their presence, but attending to these very people, seeking their advice in essential matters, and working in association with them alone. Why? The ayah itself gives the reason: they call on their Lord morning and evening, *yurīdūna wajhah* — "seeking His Face," wanting Allah's pleasure alone. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that these are precisely the conditions that attract the help and support of Allah; such people need not worry about losing worldly backing, for the final victory shall be theirs. Ibn Kathir describes who they are in practice: those who remember Allah, who say "La Ilaha Illallah," who praise, glorify, and magnify Him morning and evening — all the servants of Allah, whether rich or poor, strong or weak.

A parallel moment is preserved in the Sunnah. Imam Muslim recorded in his Sahih that Saʿd bin Abi Waqqas said: "There was a group of six of us with the Prophet ﷺ. The idolators said, 'Tell these people to leave so they will not offend us.' There was myself, Ibn Masʿud, a man from Hudayl, Bilal and two other men whose names I have forgotten. Allah's Messenger ﷺ thought to himself about whatever Allah willed he should think about, then Allah revealed: 'And turn not away those who invoke their Lord, morning and afternoon' (6:52)." Ibn Kathir notes that only Muslim reported this, not al-Bukhari. The Qur'an intervened before the thought could even become a decision.

The rest of ayah 28 turns to the other side of the bargain. "Let not your eyes overlook them, desiring the pomp and glitter of the life of the world" — Ibn ʿAbbas explained: do not favor others over them; do not seek the people of nobility and wealth instead of them. "And obey not him whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance" — those, Ibn Kathir says, whom this world has distracted from religion and from worshipping their Lord. And the closing verdict on such a person: *wa-kāna amruhu furuṭā*, "his affair has been lost" — his actions and deeds, Ibn Kathir writes, are a foolish waste of time. Do not obey him, do not admire his way, do not envy what he has. Ibn Kathir pairs this with 20:131: "strain not your eyes in longing for the things We have given for enjoyment to various groups of them, the splendor of the life of this world, that We may test them thereby. But the provision of your Lord is better and more lasting." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out why the chiefs' advice had to be refused: their hearts were heedless of the remembrance of Allah, everything they did was subservient to their physical desires, and these conditions guaranteed that they would stand alienated far from the mercy and support of Allah.

## Truth offered, choice made real (ayah 29)

Having refused to bend the message for the powerful, the Prophet ﷺ is told exactly what to say to them: "The truth is from your Lord. Then whosoever wills, let him believe; and whosoever wills, let him disbelieve." Ibn Kathir explains the first sentence: what I have brought to you from your Lord is the truth, in which there is no confusion or doubt. And he is careful about the second: "whoever wills, let him disbelieve" is not indifference — it is, in his words, a type of threat and stern warning. The proof is what follows immediately: "Verily, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose walls will be surrounding them."

The word for those walls is *surādiq* — Ibn ʿAbbas (as reported by Ibn Jurayj) explained it simply: "a wall of fire." The chiefs who wanted an exclusive enclosure will find themselves enclosed indeed. And when its people cry for relief, "they will be granted water like *al-Muhl*, that will scald their faces." The early authorities each reached for a different image of this drink: Ibn ʿAbbas said it is thick water like the sediment in oil; Mujahid said it is like blood and pus; ʿIkrimah said it is that which is heated to the ultimate temperature; others said it is everything melted. Qatadah related that Ibn Masʿud once melted gold until it liquefied and foam rose to the top, and said: this is the thing most like al-Muhl. Ad-Dahhak said the water of Hell is black, and it itself is black, and its people are black. Ibn Kathir resolves the apparent differences beautifully: there is nothing contradictory in these comments, for al-Muhl combines all these repulsive qualities — black, evil-smelling, thick, and scalding hot. When the disbeliever brings it near to drink, it scalds his face so that the skin falls off into it. Saʿid bin Jubayr adds the fuller scene: when the people of Hell hunger, they are given the tree of Zaqqum, which tears the skin from their faces; then, thirsting, they are given this drink heated to the ultimate degree. The ayah closes: "Terrible is the drink, and an evil *murtafaq*" — an evil place to rest. Hold on to that word; the passage is about to use it again.

## The mirrored ending: ʿAdn for the sincere (ayat 30–31)

Ibn Kathir notes the deliberate structure: when Allah mentions the state of those who are doomed, He follows it by mentioning the blessed — those who believed in Allah, believed what His Messengers brought, and did the righteous deeds they were commanded. Ayah 30 opens with a guarantee: "We shall not make the reward of anyone to be lost who does his (righteous) deeds in the most perfect manner." The believers the chiefs called "broken-down" are the ones whose deeds Allah personally undertakes never to waste.

Ayah 31 then unveils their home, and Ibn Kathir walks through its vocabulary. They will have *Jannātu ʿAdn* — and ʿAdn, he says, means *lasting*. Rivers flow "beneath them," meaning beneath their rooms and dwellings (Ibn Kathir contrasts this with Firʿawn's boast, "these rivers flowing beneath me" — 43:51). They will be adorned with jewelry, bracelets of gold — elsewhere the Qur'an adds "and pearls, and their garments therein will be of silk" (22:23), which this ayah details further: green garments of *sundus* and *istabraq*. Sundus is a fine garment, like a shirt; istabraq is thick, shiny velvet. They recline *muttakiʾīn* upon *arāʾik*. On the word muttakiʾīn, Ibn Kathir explains that it implies lying down, or — the sense he judges closer to the meaning here — sitting with one's legs crossed; to illustrate the word's usage he cites a Sahih Hadith in which the Prophet ﷺ said, "As for me, I do not eat sitting with legs crossed (muttakiʾan)." And arāʾik is the plural of arīkah, a bed beneath a canopy.

Then the mirror closes. Of Hell, ayah 29 said: "Terrible is the drink, and an evil murtafaq." Of Paradise, ayah 31 says: "How good is the reward, and what an excellent murtafaq!" — how good a place to dwell, rest, and stay. Ibn Kathir points out that Allah draws the same contrast in Sūrat al-Furqan: Hell is "evil as an abode and as a place to rest in" (25:66), while the believers "will be rewarded with the highest place because of their patience... excellent it is as an abode, and as a place to rest in" (25:75–76). Two resting-places, one word — and the whole passage is the choice between them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over one detail a modern reader may stumble on: gold bracelets for *men*? In this world, ornaments of gold and silk are not permissible for men — not even a gold ring or watch-chain. The answer given is that beauty and embellishment are matters of recognized custom: what one land or era counts as adornment, another finds distasteful. In Jannah, ornaments and silk will be established as the adornment of its men, and no one will find it strange. That world, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reminds us, is a universe of existence separate from everything we have experienced; it cannot be imagined on the analogy of anything around us.

## Living it

The passage legislates through a story.
