When the powerful offered the Prophet ﷺ influence in exchange for distance from the poor believers, Allah did not merely decline — He commanded the opposite: tie yourself to the people of dhikr (remembrance of Allah), and tell the powerful that the truth does not negotiate. For the believer, the applications are direct. Choose your sitting-companions by their remembrance of Allah, not their wealth or status — "whether rich or poor, strong or weak," as Ibn Kathir puts it. Do not let your eyes linger enviously on the glitter of those whose hearts are heedless; their affair, however impressive, is *furuṭ* — lost. And in conveying the religion, admit no discrimination: no VIP gatherings, no trading the dignity of humble believers for the patronage of the influential. The final ayat explain why the trade is foolish: the drink of one company scalds the face; the other company reclines on canopied couches beside flowing rivers, in a Garden whose very name means it lasts.

passages.title: The boastful owner of the two gardens
passages.tafsir:
This passage opens the parable of the two gardens: a story of a man surrounded by blessings — two flourishing gardens, wealth, and a proud entourage — who lets those very blessings convince him that he answers to no one, not even to the Hour. Ayat 32–36 form the first half of the parable: the gift, the boast, and the creed of arrogance spoken aloud. What binds them together is a single movement of the heart, traced step by step, from abundance to self-admiration to denial of the Hereafter.

## Why this parable comes here

Ibn Kathir sets the scene. The preceding ayat spoke of the idolators who were too arrogant to sit with the poor and weak among the Muslims, showing off before them with their wealth and noble lineage. Immediately after that, Allah commands His Prophet ﷺ in ayah 32: "Give them an example of two men." The parable is aimed squarely at that arrogance — Ibn Kathir titles it "The Example of the Rich Idolators and the Poor Muslims." One man stands for the wealthy deniers; his companion, as Maulana Ashraf Ali Thanavi explains in Khulasa-e-Tafsir (cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān), is a true believer of lesser wealth. The rich man of the story is not merely a character; he is a mirror held up to every heart that reads worldly success as proof of standing with Allah.

## The perfection of the gift (ayat 32–33)

Notice how deliberately the description is built. Allah — and the ayah stresses that it is *We* who gave — granted one of the two men two gardens of grapes, surrounded both with date palms, and placed cultivated crops between them. Ibn Kathir draws out the picture: every tree and plant abundantly fruitful, the produce readily accessible and of good quality.

Ayah 33 then adds a striking phrase: each garden "brought forth its produce and failed not in the least therein." Ibn Kathir explains: nothing at all was diminishing. And "We caused a river to gush forth in the midst of both" — Ibn Kathir notes that rivers were flowing through the gardens here and there. Everything a garden could need to flourish was present, and flourish they did, completely and without fail.

## "And he had thamar" — a word worth pausing on (ayah 34)

Ayah 34 opens: "And he had *thamar*." Ibn Kathir records two views on this word: it was said to mean wealth, and it was said to mean fruits. He inclines to "fruits" as the more apparent meaning here, supported by the variant recitation *thumr*, the plural of *thamrah* (a single fruit) — just as *khushb* is the plural of *khashab* (wood) — while others recite it *thamar*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the other side: Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and Qatadah took it in the sense of wealth, and the classical lexicon al-Qāmūs confirms the word covers both the fruit of trees and wealth of every kind. On that reading, the man did not only own gardens and farms — he also had gold, silver, and other luxuries. His own boast in the same ayah, "I am greater than you in *wealth*," supports this broader sense. Either way the picture is the same: a man surrounded on every side by what Allah had given him.

Then comes the turn. He said to his companion, "in the course of discussion" (*wa-huwa yuḥāwiruhu*) — Ibn Kathir glosses this as disputing with him, boasting, and showing off — "I am greater than you in wealth and have a mightier entourage." The word for entourage, *nafar*, Ibn Kathir explains as servants, attendants, and children: not just money, but the human retinue that money commands. Qatadah's comment on this line is cutting: "This, by Allah, is the wish of the immoral — to have a lot of wealth and a large entourage." The ambition itself, not only the boasting, is diagnosed.

## Walking into the garden, walking away from himself (ayah 35)

"And he entered his garden while wronging his own soul." The wrong here, Ibn Kathir says, was his disbelief, rebellion, arrogance, and denial of the Hereafter. Standing amid his vines he declares: "I do not think this will ever perish."

Ibn Kathir's analysis of this moment is the psychological heart of the passage. The man was allowing himself to be deceived *by what he saw* — the plants, the fruits, the trees, the rivers running through the different parts of his gardens. Because it all looked permanent, he concluded it was permanent. And Ibn Kathir names the roots of that deception: his lack of understanding, the weakness of his faith in Allah, his infatuation with this world and its adornments, and his disbelief in the Hereafter. Sight overruled faith. The eye reported abundance, and the heart, having nothing firmer to stand on, believed the eye.

## The creed of the deceived (ayah 36)

Denial of the garden's end slides, in the very next breath, into denial of everything's end: "Nor do I think the Hour will ever come." And then the most revealing sentence of all: "And if in fact I am brought back to my Lord, I will surely find better than this in return."

Ibn Kathir unpacks the logic: *if* there is a Hereafter and a return to Allah, then I will have an even better share with my Lord — "for if it were not that I am dear to Him, He would not have given me all this." The man reads his wealth as proof of divine favor. Ibn Kathir shows this is a recurring creed of the deniers, quoting Allah's words elsewhere: "But if I am brought back to my Lord, surely there will be for me the best with Him" (41:50), and "Have you seen him who disbelieved in Our Ayat and said: I shall certainly be given wealth and children?" (19:77) — an ayah revealed, Ibn Kathir notes, concerning al-ʿĀṣ bin Wāʼil. In every case the error is identical: he took it for granted that Allah would give him this, without any sound evidence.

## Why the logic fails

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, in its commentary on these very ayat, conveys Maulana Thanavi's summary of the gist of both men's arguments. The rich man's argument was exactly what ayah 36 voices: if Allah were not pleased with him, He would not have given him this amount of wealth in this world. The believing companion — whose reply the Qurʼān records in the ayat that follow — refuted it at the root: worldly wealth is not a sign of being close to Allah, because Allah gives worldly benefits, in one way or another, even to disbelievers and sinners — indeed even to snakes, scorpions, and beasts. It is a horrible mistake to presume such things are signs of divine approval. Neither the rich man's wealth proves Allah is pleased with him, nor the believer's lesser wealth proves displeasure. Allah's approval or disapproval depends on faith and deeds alone, not on the amount of wealth one has. That single principle dismantles the entire speech of ayat 34–36.

## Living it

The passage asks the believer to break the reflex it portrays: the reflex of measuring people — and oneself — by wealth and entourage, and of mistaking ease for approval. The man's downfall began not with a sin of the hand but with two sentences of the tongue: "I am greater than you," and "I do not think this will ever perish."

The sources also point to the opposite habit of the tongue. Concerning the words *mā shāʼa Allāh, lā quwwata illā billāh* — "Everything is as Allah wills; there is no power except with Allah" — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a report in Shuʿab al-Imān on the authority of Anas that the Prophet ﷺ said that whoever sees something he likes and says these words, no harm will come to it — what he likes will stay protected; other reports add that it will stay protected against the evil eye. This is the exact inversion of the garden owner's speech: where he looked at his blessings and said "mine, and forever," the believer looks at a blessing and immediately hands it back to its true Owner. That one habit — crediting Allah at the moment of admiring anything — is the practical vaccine this parable prescribes.

passages.title: The believer's rebuke and the garden's ruin
passages.tafsir:
This passage is the second half of the parable of the two gardens: the poor believer finally speaks, answering his wealthy companion's arrogance with a warning and a rebuke for his disbelief — and then everything the believer warned of comes to pass. What holds ayat 37–44 together is a single movement from word to consequence: the believer's speech (37–41) and Allah's verdict enacted in the ruined garden (42–44).

## "Do you disbelieve in Him Who created you?" (ayat 37–38)

The believer opens not with envy of his companion's wealth but with alarm at his companion's soul: "Do you disbelieve in Him Who created you out of dust, then out of a *nutfah* (a drop of fluid), then fashioned you into a man?" Ibn Kathir explains that this is a denunciation — the believer is pointing out the sheer seriousness of rejecting the Lord who formed man from dust (a reference to Adam) and then made his offspring from a humble drop of liquid. Ibn Kathir connects this to Allah's words elsewhere: "How can you disbelieve in Allah, seeing that you were dead and He gave you life?" (2:28). The argument is one every person can verify in himself: there is no one who does not know that he was nothing, then came to be — and that his existence is not due to himself or to any other creature, but to his Creator, beside Whom there is no other god.

What was the rich man's sin? Ibn Kathir describes the believer's reply as a warning and a rebuke to his companion "for his disbelief in Allah and allowing himself to be deceived." And the summary of Maulana Ashraf Ali Thanavi cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in what that disbelief consisted of: proud of his wealth, the rich man refused to accept that there is any life after death — and claimed that if there were one, he would be given even more wealth and reward there.

Against this, the believer plants his own flag in ayah 38: "But as for me: He is Allah, my Lord, and I will never associate anyone with my Lord." Ibn Kathir paraphrases: "I do not say what you say; rather I acknowledge the Oneness and Lordship of Allah" — He is the One to be worshipped alone, with no partner or associate. In two short ayat the believer affirms both truths in Ibn Kathir's twin phrases: Allah's Oneness and Lordship, and Allah as the One who alone is to be worshipped.

## The words he should have said (ayah 39)

Then comes the practical correction: "If only you had said, upon entering your garden, *mā shā' Allāh, lā quwwata illā billāh* — 'That which Allah wills! There is no power except with Allah.'"

Ibn Kathir unfolds the believer's meaning: when you entered your garden and looked at it and liked it, why did you not praise Allah for the blessings He gave you — the wealth and children He granted you and not to others — and why did you not say these words? One of the Salaf (the early generations) said, "Whoever is delighted with something in his circumstances or his wealth or his children, let him say, 'That which Allah wills! There is no power but with Allah!'" — and this practice is based on this very ayah.

The Sunnah reinforces the second half of the phrase. Ibn Kathir cites the report in the Sahih from Abu Musa that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Shall I not tell you about some of the treasure of Paradise? *Lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh* (There is no power or might but with Allah)."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a report from Shuʿab al-Imān on the authority of Sayyidna Anas that the Holy Prophet ﷺ said that whoever sees something he likes and says *mā shā' Allāhu lā quwwata illā billāh*, nothing will harm it — what he likes will stay protected. Other reports convey that reciting this phrase upon seeing something pleasing protects it against the evil eye.

Why these words? They do exactly what the rich man failed to do: they hand the blessing back to its true Owner. "That which Allah wills" confesses that the garden exists by Allah's will, not the owner's skill; "there is no power except with Allah" confesses that no one — including its owner — has any strength to preserve it.

## Wealth is not a verdict (the heart of the argument)

The believer continues: "If you see me less than you in wealth and children, perhaps my Lord will grant me something better than your garden" (39–40). Ibn Kathir specifies: something better *in the Hereafter*.

Maulana Ashraf Ali Thanavi, as cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, distills the whole debate between the two men. The rich man's unspoken logic was: if Allah were not pleased with me, He would not have given me all this wealth — and if there is a Hereafter, I will surely be given even more there. The believer demolishes this premise: worldly wealth is no sign of closeness to Allah, because Allah gives worldly benefits even to disbelievers and sinners — indeed, in one way or another, even to snakes, scorpions, and beasts. It is a horrible mistake to read provision as approval. Neither your abundance proves that Allah approves of your conduct, nor does my lesser wealth prove His disapproval. Allah's approval or disapproval depends on faith and deeds alone, never on the size of one's holdings.

This single insight is the antidote to the disease the parable diagnoses — the assumption that material success is evidence of divine favour.

## The warning: ḥusbān and ghawr (ayat 40–41)

The believer then warns what Allah could do to the garden its owner thought eternal: "He may send upon it *ḥusbān* from the sky, so that it becomes a slippery barren earth; or its water may sink into the ground, and you will never be able to seek it out."

Two rare words carry the threat, and the commentators dwell on both:

**Ḥusbān.** Ibn ʿAbbas, Ad-Dahhak and Qatadah said — and Malik narrated from Az-Zuhri — that it means a punishment from heaven. Ibn Kathir judges the apparent meaning to be a mighty rain that would tear up the garden's plants and trees. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the range of early views: Qatadah explained it as punishment in an absolute sense, Ibn ʿAbbas as *fire*, and some as stoning. The garden would then become *ṣaʿīdan zalaqan* — in Ibn Kathir's words, smooth mud in which one cannot get a foothold; Ibn ʿAbbas said, "Like land without vegetation, where nothing grows." The image is total: not a damaged orchard but slick, lifeless ground.

**Ghawr.** "Or its water becomes *ghawran*" — it vanishes downward into the earth, the opposite of flowing water that seeks the surface. Ibn Kathir notes that Allah uses the same word elsewhere: "Say: Tell me! If your water were to sink away, who then could bring you flowing water?" (67:30). He adds a fine linguistic point: *ghawr* is from the same root as *ghā'ir* ("sinking") but is more intensive — the water is not merely low, it is gone beyond all retrieval: "you will never be able to seek it."

The two threats cover both directions: destruction from above (the sky) and loss from below (the water table). A garden lives suspended between rain and springs; Allah holds both.

## The ruin (ayat 42–43)

Ayah 42 opens with a passive verb of quiet finality: *wa-uḥīṭa bi-thamarihi* — "his fruits were encircled" with ruin, struck from all sides. Ibn Kathir notes that *thamar* here means his wealth, or on the other view his crops; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid and Qatadah, and the lexicon al-Qāmūs) explains that the word covers both the fruit of trees and wealth of every kind — so the man lost not only his gardens and farms but the gold, silver and luxuries that went with them. What this disbeliever was afraid of, and what the believer had warned him of, actually happened: a storm struck the garden he had erroneously thought would last forever — the very garden that had distracted him from thoughts of Allah, may He be glorified. As for what the calamity was, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes that the Qur'an does not name it explicitly; it appears that fire came down from the sky and consumed everything, in line with Ibn ʿAbbas's explanation of *ḥusbān* as fire — and Allah knows best.

Then the Qur'an gives us his posture: "he began to turn his palms over what he had spent on it, while it lay in ruins upon its trellises." Qatadah said: "He was clasping his hands together in a gesture of regret and grief for the wealth he had lost." The detail "over what he had spent upon it" is pointed — he grieves not only the garden but the lifetime of investment sunk into it.

And his only words now: "Would that I had never associated anyone with my Lord!" The very confession the believer had urged on him in ease, he utters in ruin — too late for the garden, wrung out of him by loss.

Ayah 43 completes the stripping: "And he had no group of men to help him against Allah, nor could he defend himself." Ibn Kathir explains that the *fi'ah* (group, band of supporters) means the clan or children he had vainly boasted of. The man who had boasted "I am greater than you in wealth" now finds that when Allah's decree arrives, wealth is gone and men are useless.

## "There, all protection belongs to Allah, the True" (ayah 44)

The passage closes with the verdict: *hunālika al-walāyatu lillāhi al-ḥaqq* — "There, al-Walayah is for Allah, the True God. He is best in reward and best in final outcome."

Ibn Kathir records that the reciters differed over this ayah in ways that enrich rather than contradict each other:

- **Where to pause.** Some pause after *hunālika* ("there"), attaching it to the previous phrase: "nor could he defend himself *there*" — that is, at that moment, when Allah sends His punishment, no one can save him. Others pause before it, reading "There, al-Walayah belongs to Allah" — at that moment of ruin, all help and protection is Allah's alone.
- **Al-walāyah or al-wilāyah.** Read as *al-walāyah*, the sense is allegiance: on that Day everyone, believer and disbeliever alike, will turn to Allah in submission when the punishment comes to pass — as Allah says of the nations, "When they saw Our punishment, they said: 'We believe in Allah alone'" (40:84), and of Firʿawn, who cried out his belief only as the drowning overtook him and was told, "Now? While you refused to believe before?" (10:90–91). Read as *al-wilāyah*, the sense is rule and sovereignty: on that Day dominion belongs to Allah, the True — as in "The sovereignty on that Day will be the true sovereignty, belonging to the Most Gracious" (25:26).
- **Al-ḥaqq.** Some read it as describing the wilāyah — the *true* sovereignty; others read it as a name of Allah Himself, may He be glorified — "the True," as in "Then they are returned to Allah, their True Protector" (6:62).

Every reading converges on the same lesson the ruined garden has just taught: when the decree falls, there is no protector, no ally, and no king except Allah.

And the final words lift the eye from the wreckage to the alternative: "He is best in reward and best in final outcome (*ʿuqbā*)." Ibn Kathir comments: for deeds done for the sake of Allah, the reward is good and the consequences are all good. The rich man's garden ended as slippery mud; what is stored with Allah does not fail.

## Living it

The passage leaves the believer with concrete practices, all drawn directly from its ayat:

- **Say *mā shā' Allāh, lā quwwata illā billāh* over what delights you** — your home, wealth, children, work — as the Salaf advised on the basis of ayah 39. It is the verbal act of returning the blessing to its Owner, and the reports cited in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān connect it with the blessing's protection.
- **Treasure *lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh*** — the Prophet ﷺ called it a treasure of Paradise.
- **Never read wealth as a verdict** — neither your abundance as Allah's approval nor another's poverty as His displeasure. His approval rests on faith and deeds alone.
- **Speak up as the believer did.** He was the poorer man, yet he warned and rebuked his companion for his disbelief and for allowing himself to be deceived — loyalty to truth over deference to wealth.

The rich man wanted a garden that would last forever; he lost it. The believer wanted his Lord; and "He is best in reward and best in final outcome."

passages.title: This worldly life is like fleeting rain
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat form a single, deliberate contrast: first a parable that shows what this worldly life really is — rain, green growth, then dry and broken pieces scattered by the wind — and then the verdict that follows from it: wealth and children are only the *adornment* of that fleeting life, while "the good righteous deeds that last" are what truly hold their value with Allah. Ayah 45 gives the image; ayah 46 draws the conclusion.

## The parable: a whole lifetime in one rainfall

In ayah 45 Allah commands His Prophet ﷺ: "And give them a parable of this worldly life." Ibn Kathir explains that the point of the parable is the dunya's **transient nature — how it will eventually cease and come to an end**. Water comes down from the sky; it mingles with the seeds already lying in the earth, and they grow and become good, "producing bright, fresh flowers." Then, with no long interval, the same vegetation "becomes dry and broken pieces" — withered up — and the winds scatter it, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "tossing them about right and left."

Notice how the ayah compresses the whole cycle. It moves straight from lush green to *hashīm* — the "dry and broken pieces" of the ayah's own wording — dead plant matter that cannot even hold together against the wind. The freshness was real, but it was never the plant's own possession; it lasted exactly as long as Allah willed and not a moment longer. That is the dunya: genuinely attractive, genuinely green — and incapable of lasting.

The ayah closes: "And Allah is able to do everything" — وَكَانَ اللَّهُ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ مُّقْتَدِرًا. Ibn Kathir's comment is brief and pointed: "He has the power to do this and that" — the One who brings the greenery out is the same One who reduces it to broken pieces. Neither the flourishing nor the withering happens on its own.

## A parable Allah repeats — and why

Ibn Kathir observes that the Qur'an often gives parables like this of the life of this world, and he gathers the parallels: Surah Yunus (10:24), where the rain-fed produce feeds "men and cattle" before its end; Surah az-Zumar (39:21), where the water penetrates the earth and brings out "crops of different colors"; and Surah al-Hadid (57:20), where the life of this world is "play and amusement, pomp and mutual boasting among you, and rivalry in respect of wealth and children," likened to vegetation after rain whose growth pleases the tiller. The repetition is itself instructive: this is the Qur'an's settled picture of the dunya, not a passing metaphor.

Alongside these ayat, Ibn Kathir cites the same picture in the Sahih Hadith: **"This world is sweet and green"** (الدُّنْيَا حُلْوَةٌ خَضِرَةٌ). This concedes the parable's first half — the dunya really is sweet, really is green. The danger is not that its beauty is fake; it is that the green stage is followed, always, by the *hashīm* stage.

## Ayah 46: adornment versus what lasts

Having shown what the dunya is, ayah 46 names its two most beloved contents: "Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world." *Zīnah* — adornment — is decoration, not substance. Ibn Kathir links this to 3:14, "Beautified for men is the love of things they covet; women, children, vaulted hoards of gold…", and to 64:15: "Your wealth and your children are only a trial, whereas Allah! With Him is a great reward." His practical conclusion: turning towards Allah and worshipping Him is better for you than keeping busy with wealth and children, accumulating for them, and "going to extremes in feeling pity and compassion for them."

Against the adornment stands الْبَاقِيَاتُ الصَّالِحَاتُ — *al-bāqiyāt al-ṣāliḥāt*, the good righteous deeds that last. And they are better on two counts the ayah spells out: better **with your Lord for reward** and better **for hope** — a person's hopes are more safely pinned on them than on any estate or heir.

## What are "the deeds that last"? The Salaf answer

The early authorities gave several answers, and the sources present them as complementary rather than competing:

- **The five daily prayers.** Ibn Kathir reports this from Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid bin Jubayr and others among the Salaf; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the same from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Masruq and Ibrahim.
- **The words of remembrance.** ʿAtaʼ bin Abi Rabah and Saʿid bin Jubayr narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that they are *Subḥān Allāh* (glory be to Allah), *al-Ḥamdu lillāh* (praise be to Allah), *Lā ilāha illallāh* (there is none worthy of worship except Allah), and *Allāhu Akbar* (Allah is Most Great). When ʿUthman bin ʿAffan, the Commander of the Faithful, was asked which deeds these are, he gave the same words and added *Lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh il-ʿAliyyil-ʿAẓīm* — "there is no strength and no power except with Allah the Exalted, the Almighty." This was recorded by Imam Ahmad. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this tafsir — that the verse means the very recitation of these words — is reported from Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrimah and Mujahid; and al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas simply: "They are good words."
- **All righteous deeds.** In the report of ʿAli bin Abi Talhah, Ibn ʿAbbas included the words of dhikr *and* fasting, prayer, Hajj, charity, freeing slaves, jihad, maintaining ties of kinship, "and all other good deeds… which will remain in Paradise for those who do them for as long as heaven and earth remain." ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam said simply, "They are all righteous deeds." Ibn Kathir notes that this was also the view chosen by Ibn Jarir, may Allah have mercy on him.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records this broad reading too: another report from Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbas explains the "everlasting virtues" as righteous deeds in a general sense — including the words of dhikr, the five prayers, and all other righteous deeds — an explanation also reported from the early commentator Qatadah. And Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the very wording of the Qur'an drives towards this meaning, for the words literally convey the sense of righteous deeds **that are to keep surviving** — and every deed that is righteous and sincere is abiding and everlasting in the sight of Allah. It is for this reason, it notes, that Ibn Jarir and al-Qurtubi preferred this particular tafsir.

## From the Sunnah

The sources anchor the dhikr-interpretation in the Prophet's ﷺ own words:

- Imam Ahmad recorded from a freed slave of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he said: "Well done! Well done for five things! How heavy they will weigh in the balance: *Lā ilāha illallāh*, *Allāhu Akbar*, *Subḥān Allāh*, *al-Ḥamdu lillāh*, and a righteous son who dies and his parents seek the reward of Allah" — and: "Well done! Well done for five things! Whoever meets Allah believing in them will enter Paradise: belief in Allah, the Last Day, Paradise and Hell, resurrection after death, and the Reckoning."
- The Musnad of Ahmad, Ibn Hibban and Hakim report from Sayyidna Abu Saʿid al-Khudri that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Accumulate 'everlasting virtues' as much as you can." Asked what they are, he named these same words of glorification. Hakim called this hadith sahih.
- The Sahih of Muslim and Tirmidhi report from Sayyidna Abu Hurairah that the Prophet ﷺ said he likes saying *Subḥān Allāh, al-Ḥamdu lillāh, Lā ilāha illallāh, Allāhu Akbar* "better than everything under the Sun."
- Al-ʿUqaili reports the same identification of the "everlasting virtues" from Sayyidna Nuʿman ibn Bashir, and al-Tabarani the same from Sayyidna Saʿd ibn ʿUbadah.
- Sayyidna Jabir said: "Recite *lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh* a lot, because it removes ninety-nine types of ailments, out of which anxiety is the least painful."

Two sayings from the early generations complete the picture. Sayyidna ʿAli said: "Cultivation is of two kinds. Wealth and children are the cash crops of the mortal world, while 'everlasting virtues' are the deferred crops of the Hereafter" — turning the rain-parable itself into counsel: choose which harvest you are farming for. And Hasan al-Basri said the everlasting virtues are one's **intention**, "as the acceptance of righteous deeds depends on it."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing al-Qurtubi) also relays the view of ʿUbaid ibn ʿUmair that righteous **daughters** are among the everlasting virtues — "the greatest treasure-troves of reward" for their parents — supported by a narration of Sayyidah ʿAʼishah according to which the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have described a man of his ummah under orders to be taken to Hell, whose righteous daughters clung to him, pleading: O Allah, spare him, for he was very kind to us and worked very hard to raise us — and Allah, in His mercy, forgave him. Read alongside ayah 46, the point is exact: children as *adornment* — status, pride, worldly delight — belong to the grass that withers; but children raised righteously become part of what remains.

## Living it

The passage does not tell the believer to abandon wealth and family; it tells him what category they belong to. Adornment is enjoyed, but nothing is built on it. What the ayat concretely commend is cheap, portable, and available to everyone at any moment: the five prayers guarded, and the tongue kept moist with *Subḥān Allāh, al-Ḥamdu lillāh, Lā ilāha illallāh, Allāhu Akbar, lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh* — words the Prophet ﷺ said he likes "better than everything under the Sun," and which, unlike the green of the dunya, will still be standing when the wind has taken everything else.

passages.title: Mountains blown away and the record laid open
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are a single, unbroken scene of the Day of Resurrection: the earth stripped bare, every human being who ever lived standing in rows before their Lord, and the record of deeds laid open. What holds them together is a steady narrowing of focus: from the cosmos — the mountains blown away and the earth levelled — to the assembled rows of humanity, to the single open Book in which nothing, however small, has been missed. Ibn Kathir treats the whole passage as one unit under a single heading, "The Major Terrors of the Hour": Allah, he says, here tells us of "the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, and the awesome things that will come to pass."

## An earth with nowhere to hide

The scene opens with the mountains — the very symbol of permanence — set in motion. Ibn Kathir reads this alongside its sister passages: elsewhere Allah says the heaven will shake and "the mountains pass moving away" (52:9–10), meaning "they will move from their places and will vanish"; that you see the mountains and "think them solid, but they shall pass away as the passing away of the clouds" (27:88); that they will be "like carded wool" (101:5); and that "My Lord will pulverize them scattering their dust, to leave them as a barren plain… you will not see in it crookness or curve" (20:105–107). Reading these together, Ibn Kathir concludes that the mountains will vanish and the earth will be left "a smooth plain, a level surface with nothing crooked or curved therein, no valleys or mountains."

That is the force of the word *bāriza* — the earth laid bare, levelled and exposed. Ibn Kathir explains it as "clear and open, with no features that anyone may recognize and nothing for anyone to hide behind. All creatures will be visible to their Lord, and not one of them will be hidden from Him." The early commentators he cites compress it into two remarks: Mujahid and Qatadah said, "No one will be hidden or absent," and Qatadah said, "There will be no buildings and no trees." The flattening of the earth is not scenery for its own sake; it is the physical form of total accountability. Every landmark behind which a person might shelter — or hide — is gone.

Then: "We shall gather them so that We will not leave one of them behind." Ibn Kathir glosses this as "the first of them and the last of them… We shall not leave anyone behind, young or old," and again lets the Qur'an explain the Qur'an: "those of old, and those of later times, all will surely be gathered together for an appointed meeting of a known Day" (56:49–50); "that is a Day whereon mankind will be gathered together, and that is a Day when all will be present" (11:103). No generation, no individual, is outside this summons.

## Standing in rows, exactly as first created

On that levelled plain the gathered creation is now presented: "And they will be set before your Lord, aligned." Ibn Kathir notes that the word *ṣaffan* ("aligned," "in a row") can be read in two ways, and he attributes both rather than deciding between them: it may mean that all of creation will stand before Allah in one row — as in "the Day that Ar-Rūḥ (Jibril) and the angels will stand aligned" (78:38) — or that they will stand in rows, as in "and your Lord comes with the angels in rows" (89:22). Either way the picture is of ordered, inescapable presentation before the Judge.

Then comes the address: "Now indeed, you have come to Us as We created you the first time. Nay, but you thought that We had appointed no meeting for you." Ibn Kathir reads this as "a rebuke to those who denied the Hereafter, a reprimand before all creation" — you did not think this would happen to you or come to pass, and here you stand at the appointment you denied.

**"As We created you the first time" — literally.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills out this phrase with a moving scene from the Sunnah. Al-Bukhari, Muslim and Tirmidhi report on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas that the Prophet ﷺ once said in a khutbah: "O people! On the Day of Qiyamah, you will come walking bare-footed, bare-bodied, before your Lord and the one to be donned with a dress first shall be Ibrahim, peace be on him." Hearing this, ʿA'ishah asked: Messenger of Allah, is it that all men and women shall be naked, and seeing each other? He answered that on that Day everyone will be gripped by such preoccupation and anxiety that no one will have any occasion to cast a look towards anyone — all eyes shall be raised upwards. The terror of the Day will do what no garment could.

Maʿārif — drawing on al-Qurtubi and on the tafsir work Mazhari, which its author cites here — then addresses an apparent tension with other reports: that the dead meet one another in Barzakh (the state between death and resurrection) dressed in their shrouds, and ʿUmar's advice, "Give good kafn (shroud) to the deceased among you because they will rise on the Last Day dressed in these." The reconciliations offered: al-Qurtubi says the shroud reports concern the Grave and Barzakh, not the plains of Resurrection itself; some commentators restrict them to martyrs, who are buried in their dress; and others say it is possible that some rise dressed on the Day of Resurrection and some without, so that both kinds of report conjoin. This is a place where the transmitted texts genuinely pull in different directions, and the scholars harmonised rather than discarded.

## The Book that missed nothing

The rebuke to the deniers is now given its evidence: "And the Book will be produced." Ibn Kathir identifies it as the Book of deeds, "which contains a record of everything, major or minor, significant or insignificant, great or small." At the sight of it the criminals (*al-mujrimūn*) are *mushfiqīn* — fearful of what is in it, Ibn Kathir says, "of their evil deeds and reprehensible actions." Their cry — "Woe to us!" — is, in his words, an expression of "regret for having wasted their lives." And their astonished question captures what makes the Book terrifying: "What sort of Book is this that leaves neither a small thing nor a large thing, but has recorded it with numbers!" It has left no sin, major or minor, and no action however small, "but it has recorded it with the utmost precision and accuracy."

Notice who is speaking. The deniers who once assumed no appointment had been set now become the Book's most emphatic witnesses — their protest is itself testimony to its completeness.

"And they will find all that they did, present." Ibn Kathir links this to the wider Qur'anic theme that nothing done in secret survives as a secret: "on the Day when every person will be confronted with all the good he has done" (3:30), "man will be informed of what he sent forward, and what he left behind" (75:13), and "the Day when all the secrets will be exposed" (86:9) — everything hidden in people's hearts will become known. He then cites the hadith recorded by Imam Ahmad from Anas that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Every traitor will have a banner on the Day of Resurrection, by which he will be known." It was also narrated in the Two Sahihs, where one narration says: "On the Day of Resurrection, for every traitor a banner will be erected by his backside, and it will be said, 'This is the betrayer of so-and-so the son of so-and-so.'" Even treachery, the most concealed of sins, is publicly labelled that Day.

## "Your Lord treats no one with injustice" — down to a slap

The passage of terrors ends not with wrath but with justice. Ibn Kathir: Allah "will judge between His creatures for all of their deeds, and He will not treat any of His creatures with injustice. He will overlook and forgive and have mercy, and He will punish whomever He wills by His power, wisdom and justice… He is the Judge Who never wrongs or oppresses." He pairs this with "Surely, Allah wrongs not even of the weight of a speck of dust, but if there is any good, He doubles it" (4:40) and the Balances of justice in 21:47. Note the asymmetry Ibn Kathir draws out from 4:40: wrong is never inflated, but good is multiplied.

How exact is this justice? Ibn Kathir relates the story recorded by Imam Ahmad: Jabir bin ʿAbdullah was told about a hadith which a man — ʿAbdullah bin Unays — had heard from the Prophet ﷺ and which Jabir himself had not heard directly. Jabir bought a camel and travelled a full month to Ash-Sham for the sake of that one hadith, fearing "that you or I would die before I could hear it." The hadith he crossed the desert for is about this very scene: Allah will gather the people — or His servants — on the Day of Resurrection naked, uncircumcised and *buhman*, meaning having nothing with them. Then a voice will call out to them, heard by those far away just as easily as by those near: "I am the Sovereign, I am the Judge. None of the people of Hell should enter Hell if he is owed something by one of the people of Paradise, until I have settled the matter, and none of the people of Paradise should enter Paradise if he is owed something by one of the people of Hell, until I settle the matter — even if it is only the case of a slap." The Companions asked how that could be, when they would come before Allah barefooted, naked and having nothing; he ﷺ answered: "By [merit for] good deeds, and [recompense] for evil deeds" — the only currency left. And the justice reaches past mankind altogether: in the narration from ʿUthman bin ʿAffan recorded by ʿAbdullah the son of Imam Ahmad, the Prophet ﷺ said the animal who lost a horn will settle the score with the one that has horns on the Day of Resurrection.

## "They will find what they did, present" — the deed becomes the recompense

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān preserves here a striking insight from the author's teacher, Maulana Sayyid Muhammad Anwar Shah Kashmiri. Commentators generally supply an ellipsis: they will find *the recompense of* their deeds present. Kashmiri used to say no such interpretation is needed. Countless hadith narratives prove that the very deeds of this world will become the recompense — reward or punishment — of the Hereafter; their forms will transform there. Righteous deeds will transform into the blessings of Paradise, and evil deeds will turn into the Hellfire, snakes and scorpions. It appears in hadith that the wealth of those who do not pay zakah will come to them in the grave in the form of a big snake, biting them and saying, "I am your wealth"; that the righteous deed, transformed into an elegant human visitor, will come to mollify the terrible loneliness of the grave; that sacrificial animals will provide the ride over the Bridge of Sirat; and that sins committed will be placed on top of their doers' heads as their burden on the Day of Resurrection.

On this reading, verses like "they only eat fire into their bellies" — said of those who devour the orphans' property unjustly (4:10) — need no figure of speech. It really is fire even now; only the experience of its effect awaits the next world — the way a matchbox may truthfully be called fire, though it takes friction to show it, or petrol may be called fire, though it takes a tiny flame to prove it. Whatever good or bad a person does in this world will simply appear in the Hereafter in its true form. And Allah alone knows best.

## What the passage asks of you

The Qur'an addresses this scene to "you" — "you will see the earth as a levelled plain," "you will see the criminals, fearful." The reader is not being told about other people; he is being placed on that plain. Three things follow directly from the texts here. First, nothing is too small to matter: the Book the criminals dread is dreadful precisely because it kept the small things, and Allah's justice reaches down to the case of a single slap — so the small wrongs owed to others are worth settling now, while deeds are still the currency in our own hands. Second, secrecy is temporary: on an earth with no buildings, no trees, and nothing to hide behind, the only deeds worth accumulating are ones you would be content to find "present" before you. And third, the same exactness cuts the other way — a Lord who wrongs no one by even the weight of a speck of dust, and doubles whatever good there is, has made the smallest good deed as indestructible as the smallest sin.

passages.title: Iblis's defiance and the failure of false allies
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a single sustained argument against taking anyone as an ally in place of Allah. It opens in ayah 50 with Iblis's refusal to prostrate to Adam — the enmity of Iblis towards the Children of Adam and their father before them — then asks the devastating question that gives the whole unit its point: after all this, will you really take *him* and his offspring as your protectors instead of Me? Ayah 51 dismantles any claim such false allies could have to power, and ayat 52–53 fast-forward to the Day of Resurrection, when those so-called partners are called and cannot answer, and their followers stand before the Fire with no way out. The passage moves from the beginning of the story to its end so the reader can see the full arc of a terrible bargain.

## The story of Adam and Iblis — and why it is retold here

Ibn Kathir explains why the story of Adam and Iblis appears at this point in Surat al-Kahf: Allah is reminding the Children of Adam of the enmity of Iblis towards them and their father before them, and rebuking those who follow him against their Creator. It is Allah who created them from nothing and sustains them by His kindness — yet some still take Iblis as a friend and set themselves against Allah. The command in ayah 50, "Prostrate before Adam," was addressed to all the angels, as Ibn Kathir notes with reference to the fuller account at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah. And the prostration itself was one of respect and honour towards Adam — not worship — as shown by Allah's words elsewhere: "when I have fashioned him completely and breathed into him the soul... then fall down prostrating yourselves unto him" (15:28–29).

## "He was one of the Jinn" — nature shows itself under pressure

The ayah itself answers an obvious question: if the command was given to the angels, how could one of them refuse? Allah says of Iblis, *kāna min al-jinn* — "he was one of the Jinn." Ibn Kathir comments that his original nature betrayed him: he had been created from smokeless fire, whereas the angels were created from light. He cites the hadith in Sahih Muslim, from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The angels were created from light, Iblis was created from smokeless fire, and Adam was created from that which has been described to you."

Ibn Kathir draws a piercing lesson from this: "When matters are crucial, every vessel leaks that which it contains and is betrayed by its true nature." Iblis used to do what the angels did and resembled them in devotion and worship — which is why he was included in the address to them — but when the moment of testing came, what he really was came out. His own argument condemned him: "I am better than he. You created me from fire, and You created him from clay" (38:76).

Was Iblis ever an angel at all? Al-Hasan al-Basri said plainly: "Iblis was not one of the angels, not even for a second. He was the origin of the Jinn just as Adam, upon him be peace, was the origin of mankind." Ibn Kathir records that Ibn Jarir narrated this with a sahih (authentic) chain.

## The word *fasaqa* — stepping out of bounds

The ayah says Iblis *fasaqa* — "he disobeyed the command of his Lord." Ibn Kathir opens up the Arabic: *fisq* carries the root sense of going out, stepping beyond a boundary. Arabs used the same verb for a date emerging from its flower, and for a mouse coming out of its hole to do damage. So the word paints a picture: Iblis did not merely fail to obey; he *broke out* of the bounds of obedience to Allah altogether — like something that leaves its proper place in order to cause harm.

## "Him and his offspring" — does Shaytan have progeny?

The rebuke that follows names not only Iblis but *dhurriyyatahu* — "his offspring." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on this word. Some commentators said that "progeny" here means his accomplices — the hosts and helpers who do his work — and that literal offspring from his loins is not a necessary reading. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also cites a sahih hadith reported by Humaidi in Kitab al-Jam' bain al-Sahihain, on the authority of Salman al-Farisi (may Allah be pleased with him), in which the Prophet ﷺ told him not to be among the first to enter the bazaar or the last to leave it, "for the bazaar is a place where the Shaitan has his eggs and offspring laid around." On the basis of this, al-Qurtubi concluded that Shaytan's having accomplices and armies is established by conclusive proofs, and that his having offspring is supported by this sahih hadith — adding, "Allah knows best." Either way, the point of the ayah stands: Iblis does not work alone, and hostility to the Children of Adam is a family enterprise.

## The question at the heart of the passage

Now comes the sentence everything has been building towards: "Will you then take him and his offspring as protectors and helpers rather than Me, while they are enemies to you?" Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah's rebuke of those who obey Iblis: knowing his history, knowing his declared enmity, they still made him their *wali* — their protector and ally — in place of the One who created and sustains them. Hence the verdict that closes ayah 50: "What an evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers." The word "exchange" is exact: they traded the friendship of their Creator for the friendship of their declared enemy. Ibn Kathir compares this to the scene in Surah Ya Sin where, after the terrors of the Resurrection are described, the criminals are told to stand apart and are asked, "Did you not then understand?" (36:59–62).

## Ayah 51 — the false allies witnessed nothing, not even their own creation

Ayah 51 strips these substitute protectors of any claim to power. Ibn Kathir paraphrases Allah's argument: those whom you take as helpers instead of Me are creatures just like you. They possess nothing. They did not witness the creation of the heavens and the earth — nor even their own creation — because they did not exist at that time. Allah alone independently and exclusively creates and controls all things, with no partner, associate, or advisor. Ibn Kathir supports this with the ayah: "Call upon those you claim besides Allah; they possess not even a speck of dust in the heavens or on the earth, nor have they any share in either, nor is there for Him any assistant among them" (34:22–23).

The ayah ends: "nor did I take those who mislead as *ʿadud*." Malik explained *ʿadud* as "assistants." Allah has never needed helpers — least of all misleaders. Whoever serves Iblis, then, serves someone who had no hand in creation, no share in power, and no standing with Allah.

## Ayat 52–53 — the day the partners fail

The passage now leaps to the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir describes the scene: Allah will address the idolators before all of creation, rebuking them: "Call those so-called partners of Mine whom you claimed" — that is, the partners you claimed in the world; call them *today* to save you from the situation you are in. Ibn Kathir sets alongside this the ayah, "And truly, you have come unto Us alone as We created you the first time... Now all relations between you and them have been cut off, and all that you used to claim has vanished from you" (6:94).

"Then they will cry unto them, but they will not answer them." The silence is total — as in the parallel ayat Ibn Kathir cites: "Call upon those partners of yours; then they will call upon them, but they will not answer them" (28:64), and the false gods will not merely fail their worshippers but turn against them: "Nay, but they will deny their worship of them, and become opponents to them" (19:81–82).

**The Mawbiq.** "And We shall put Mawbiq between them." Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others explained *mawbiq* as "destruction." On this reading, the idolators will have no way of reaching the gods they claimed: Allah will separate the two parties in the Hereafter, with devastation, great horrors and terrible things between them, so neither can reach the other. 'Abdullah bin 'Amr understood the pronoun "between them" differently — as referring to the believers and the disbelievers: the people of guidance and the people of misguidance will be decisively separated on that Day. Ibn Kathir notes that this second reading matches ayat such as "on the Day when the Hour will be established — that Day shall all men be separated" (30:14) and "O you criminals! Get you apart this Day from the believers" (36:59). Both readings are transmitted from the early authorities, and both converge on the same reality: every false alliance is severed on that Day.

**Seeing the Fire.** Ayah 53 completes the scene: "The criminals shall see the Fire and apprehend that they are to fall therein, and they will find no way of escape from it." Ibn Kathir describes them seeing Hell with their own eyes as it is dragged forth by seventy thousand reins, each pulled by seventy thousand angels. At that moment they realize that being thrown into it is inevitable — and Ibn Kathir adds a searching observation: that realization *itself* intensifies their anguish, "because the anticipation and fear of punishment is in itself a real punishment." There is no *masrif* — no way of turning aside, no route of flight.

## Living it

The passage asks one question of the reader, and asks it twice — once at the beginning of the story and once at its end. In ayah 50: knowing who Iblis is and what he did, will you take him and his offspring as allies instead of Allah? In ayat 52–53: and if you do, where will those allies be when you need them most? Ibn Kathir's framing makes the practical thrust plain: Allah created us from nothing and sustains us by His kindness; to give our loyalty and obedience to His enemy is not neutrality but the very trade the ayah condemns — "What an evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers." The passage also leaves a quieter warning in Ibn Kathir's remark about Iblis: outward resemblance to the devout is no guarantee — "every vessel leaks that which it contains" when the moment of testing comes. What matters is not looking like the obedient but obeying when the command actually falls on you.

# Why People Reject Guidance Despite Every Example (18:54–59)

This passage answers a question that hangs over the whole story of revelation: if the truth is so clear, why do people still refuse it? Ayah 54 states that Allah has left nothing out — every kind of example has been set forth in this Qur'an — and then names the real obstacle: not a lack of evidence, but something inside the human being, an appetite for argument. The ayat that follow trace where that argumentativeness leads: demanding to *see* the punishment rather than believe the warning, fighting truth with falsehood and mockery, turning away even after being reminded — and then the passage closes by holding two realities together: a Lord who is All-Forgiving and Full of Mercy, and an appointed time from which there is no escape. What binds these six ayat into one unit is a single diagnosis: guidance has already arrived in full; what remains is the human response, and the clock that is running on it.

## The diagnosis: every example given — and still the arguing

Allah opens: *"We have surely set forth in this Qur'an every kind of lesson."* Ibn Kathir explains the meaning: in this Qur'an Allah has explained matters to mankind and given clear details **so that they will not stray from the truth or be misled from the path of guidance**. The case has been made completely. Yet the ayah ends with a devastating observation: *man is ever more quarrelsome than anything* — despite the explanation, Ibn Kathir says, man "opposes truth with falsehood, except for those whom Allah guides to the path of salvation." The ayah does not say man lacks intelligence or evidence; it says he is quarrelsome. The problem is not in the proof but in the receiver.

**A scene from the Prophet's ﷺ own household.** Ibn Kathir records — from Imam Ahmad, and it is also in the Two Sahihs — that ʿAli ibn Abi Talib said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came at night to visit him and Fatimah, the daughter of Allah's Messenger, and said, *"Are you not going to pray?"* ʿAli answered: "O Messenger of Allah, our souls are in the Hand of Allah. If He wills to wake us, He will wake us." The Prophet ﷺ went away without replying — and then ʿAli heard him, as he walked off, slapping his thigh and reciting: *"But, man is ever more quarrelsome than anything."*

The Prophet ﷺ answered that reply not with a rebuke but with this very ayah. Ibn Kathir places the incident here as a living illustration of the trait the ayah names — a reminder that the readiness to argue is a human trait, one that even the noblest household must be alert to.

**How far arguing can go: a scene from the Day of Judgment.** Maʿārif ul-Qurʼān cites, as testimony to this ayah, a hadith narrated by Sayyidna Anas — al-Qurtubi notes its subject matter is reported in Sahih Muslim — in which the Prophet ﷺ described a disbeliever brought forth on the Day of Qiyamah. Asked how he responded to the messenger sent to him, the man claims he believed in Allah and His messenger and obeyed him in everything. His book of deeds is set before him, contradicting him — he rejects the book. The witness of the angels who watched him — he rejects them too: "I do not accept their testimony... nor have I seen them." Even the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz) is shown to him — still he disputes, saying he can only accept "a witness that comes from my own person." So his mouth is sealed, and his own hands and feet bear witness against his kufr (disbelief) and shirk (associating partners with Allah), and he is thrown into the Fire.

The hadith is almost unbearable in what it reveals: human argumentativeness does not stop at death. A man will stand before his Lord, with his deeds written and angels testifying, and *still* dispute. He demanded a witness from his own person — and received one, from his own limbs. The trait ayah 54 names is not a debating habit; it is a disease that, unchecked, follows a person into the courtroom of eternity.

## Waiting for the wrong kind of proof

If every example has been given, what is actually *preventing* belief? Ayat 55 and 56 — which Ibn Kathir treats together under the heading "The Rebellion of the Disbelievers" — answer with bitter irony: nothing stands between these people and faith — and seeking their Lord's forgiveness — except that they are, in effect, waiting for one of two things: *that the way of the ancients be repeated with them, or that the torment come upon them face to face.*

Ibn Kathir explains: this is the pattern of disbelievers ancient and recent — they rejected the obvious truth even when they witnessed clear signs and proofs, and nothing stopped them from following it except their demand to witness with their own eyes the punishment they were being warned about. He then gathers the Qur'an's own record of these demands: one people told their Prophet, *"So cause a piece of the heaven to fall on us, if you are of the truthful!"* (26:187); others said, *"Bring Allah's torment upon us if you are one of the truthful"* (29:29); the Quraysh themselves prayed, *"O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones on us from the sky or bring upon us a painful torment"* (8:32); and they mocked, *"O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down! Verily, you are a madman! Why do you not bring angels to us if you are of the truthful?"* (15:6–7).

The two phrases at the end of ayah 55 are then unpacked. **"The way of the ancients" (sunnat al-awwalin)** means, in Ibn Kathir's words, "their overwhelming punishment, destroying every last one of them" — the fate of the destroyed nations repeating itself. **"The torment brought to them face to face" (qubulan)** means they see it with their own eyes, directly confronted with it. In other words: the only "proof" these people have left to receive is the one that ends the discussion permanently.

Against this demand, ayah 56 restores the correct frame: *"We do not send the Messengers except as bearers of good news and warners."* Ibn Kathir: before the punishment ever comes, the messengers give good news to those who believe in and follow them, and warnings to those who reject and oppose them. Messengers are not sent to stage punishments on demand. Their whole role is mercy-before-the-deadline.

And the ayah describes how the disbelievers meet them: they *argue with falsehood to refute the truth thereby* — they try, says Ibn Kathir, to weaken the truth the Messengers brought, "but they cannot achieve that." And worse: *"they take My Ayat and that which they are warned of in jest"* — they take the very proofs, evidences and miracles sent to warn them and make them fear the punishment, and turn them into material for mockery. Ibn Kathir's verdict on this is severe: making fun of Allah's signs "is the worst type of disbelief." There is a gradation in rejection — and treating the warning itself as a joke sits at the bottom of it.

## The worst wrong, and the sealed faculties

Ayah 57 asks: *who does more wrong than the one who is reminded of the Ayat of his Lord, then turns away from them, forgetting what his hands have sent forth?* Ibn Kathir renders the divine voice: "Who among My creatures does more wrong than one who is reminded of the signs of Allah then turns away from them" — that is, ignores them, does not listen or pay attention. And "what his hands have sent forth" means his bad deeds and evil actions — he turns from the reminder while conveniently forgetting the record he is building.

Then comes the consequence, in Allah's own words: *"Truly, We have set over their hearts akinnah... and in their ears, deafness."* **Akinnah** means coverings — veils placed over the heart, Ibn Kathir explains, "lest they should understand this Qur'an and its clear Message." The deafness in their ears, he notes, is deafness "in an abstract way, to guidance" — their physical hearing works; it is guidance specifically that no longer gets through. Hence the ayah's chilling close: *"And if you call them to guidance, even then they will never be guided."* This is the end-state of the trajectory the passage has been tracing: argue long enough against the truth, mock it persistently enough, and the very faculties for receiving it are sealed.

## Mercy holding back the deadline

Just when the passage could not sound more severe, ayah 58 turns to the Prophet ﷺ with two of Allah's names: *"And your Lord is the All-Forgiving (al-Ghafur), Owner of Mercy (Dhu al-Rahmah)."* Ibn Kathir: "your Lord, O Muhammad, is forgiving and has great mercy." *Were He to seize them for what they have earned, He would have hastened their punishment.* Ibn Kathir sets this beside its Qur'anic parallels: *"And if Allah were to punish men for that which they earned, He would not leave a moving creature on the surface of the earth"* (35:45), and *"But verily, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind in spite of their wrongdoing. And verily, your Lord is also severe in punishment"* (13:6) — noting that many ayat say the same.

So the delay these mockers interpret as proof the warning is empty is in fact the opposite: it is forbearance. Allah, says Ibn Kathir, is patient, He conceals faults and forgives sins; He may yet guide some of them from wrongdoing to true guidance. But for whoever persists in his evil ways, "there will come to him a Day when infants will turn grey and every pregnant female will shed her load." The ayah's final clause fixes it: *they have their appointed time (mawʿid), beyond which they will find no escape* — no way out, no refuge.

Ayah 59 then points to the evidence standing in plain sight: *"And these towns — We destroyed them when they did wrong, and We appointed a fixed time for their destruction."* These are the earlier nations, destroyed, Ibn Kathir says, "because of their stubborn disbelief" — each given a set time limit, "not to be increased or decreased." And he draws out the address implicit in the ayah, aimed at the idolators of every age: "The same applies to you, O idolators, so beware, or what happened to them will happen to you too — for you have rejected the noblest Messenger and greatest Prophet, and you are not dearer to Us than them, so fear My punishment and wrath."

## Living it

The passage is a mirror before it is a history lesson. Its warning is not aimed only at those who demanded stones from the sky; it names a trait — quarrelsomeness, the reflex to argue rather than submit — that the Prophet ﷺ answered with this very ayah even within his own beloved household. A few things it concretely asks of a believer:

- **When a reminder reaches you, respond — don't rebut.** The gravest wrong in ayah 57 is not ignorance but turning away *after being reminded*. The moment of hearing an ayah is a test of whether we answer it or argue with it.
- **Do not mistake respite for approval.** Ayah 58 teaches that the absence of immediate consequences is Allah's forbearance, not His indifference. There is an appointed time, and no refuge beyond it.
- **Never let sacred warnings become material for jest.** Ibn Kathir calls mockery of Allah's Ayat the worst type of disbelief; a believer keeps a guard on how he speaks of what Allah has revealed.
- **Remember "what your hands have sent forth."** The one condemned in ayah 57 turned away while forgetting his own record. Honest self-accounting — remembering our deeds while there is still time to seek forgiveness, which ayah 55 pairs with belief itself — is the opposite of that forgetting, and the door of al-Ghafur, the All-Forgiving, stands open before the appointed time arrives.
